lessons.title: Introduction
teaches: Chess is a game for two players.
Chess is a pretend battle between two armies, white and black.
White starts at the bottom of the board, black at the top.
Each army has one king, its most special piece.
The king wears a crown with a little cross on top.
You win by attacking the other king so that nothing can save him.
Term: check — the king is attacked.
Term: checkmate — the king is attacked and nothing can save him: he cannot step to a safe square, nobody can block, and nobody can catch the attacker; the game is over.
Say checkmate kindly and softly; chess is a quiet game.
Chess is very old: it began in India, travelled to Persia, then came to Europe.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Welcome to the wonderful game of chess. Chess is a game for two players, and we are going to learn it together.
Look! This is a chessboard, and these are the chess pieces. Chess is like a pretend battle between two armies.
One army is white. It starts down here, at the bottom.
The other army is black. It starts up here, at the top. The two armies face each other.
Every army has one very special piece. It is the king! Here is the white king.
And here is the black king. Each king wears a crown with a little cross on top.
Here is the big idea of chess. You win by attacking the other army's king, so that nothing can save him.
Let's watch it happen. Here is the black king, hiding behind his own pawns.
Whoosh! A white piece zooms to the top. Now it is attacking the black king. When a king is attacked, we call it check.
Can the king step to the side? No. Both side squares are on the white piece's line. If the king stepped there, he would still be attacked.
Can the king step forward? No. His own pawns are in the way. He has no safe square to step to.
Can a black piece stand in the way, to block the attack? No. Can a black piece catch the white piece? No. Nobody can help him.
The king is attacked, and nothing can save him. That is called checkmate! Checkmate means the game is over. White wins!
When you win, you can say checkmate. But say it kindly and softly. Chess players think very hard, so we keep chess a quiet game.
Chess is a very, very old game. People were playing it more than a thousand years ago!
It began long ago in India. Then it travelled to a land called Persia. Later it came to Europe, and now children all over the world play it.
Chess is a thinking game. Playing chess helps you think carefully, and it helps your memory grow strong.
Quiz time! Can you find the white king? Pause the video, and point to it.

quiz.why: Finding a piece on the start board is a looking question, not a move: the white king stands on e1.

beats.say: Here it is! In the middle of the bottom row, with a little cross on its crown. Well done!
One more. When a king is attacked, and nothing can save him, what do we call it? Have a think.

quiz.why: Naming a rule: the answer is the word checkmate.

beats.say: Checkmate! The king is attacked, and nothing can save him. He cannot step to a safe square, nobody can block, and nobody can catch the attacker. The game is over, and the other side wins.

Great job! Now you know that chess is a battle between two armies, and that you win by checkmate: attack the other king so that nothing can save him. Next time, we will explore the chessboard. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Battlefield
teaches: The chessboard is made of light and dark squares.
The board is 8 squares by 8 squares: 64 squares in all.
The corner square on your right is always light: light on the right.
Term: file — a line of squares going up and down; files are lettered a to h.
Term: rank — a line of squares going across; ranks are numbered 1 to 8.
Term: diagonal — a slanted line of squares, like a staircase.
Every square on a diagonal is the same colour.
Every square has a name: file letter first, then rank number (e.g. e4).
At the start, white fills ranks 1 and 2, and black fills ranks 7 and 8.

beats.say: Hello again, chess friends! Every battle needs a place to happen. In chess, the battle happens on the chessboard.
Here it is. The chessboard is one big square, made of lots of little squares. Some are light, and some are dark.
Let's count the squares along the bottom. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight!
Now let's count up the side. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight! Eight again.
Eight rows of eight squares make sixty four squares. That is a lot of squares!
Here is a trick for setting up the board. The corner square on your right hand side is always light. Light on the right!
Now look at this line of squares. It goes straight up and down. A line that goes up and down is called a file.
Every file has a letter. The letters are along the bottom, from A to H. This file sits above the letter E, so it is the E file.
And look at this line. It goes across, from side to side. A line that goes across is called a rank.
Every rank has a number. The numbers are up the side, from one to eight. This rank is next to number four, so it is rank four.
This line is different. It goes on a slant, from one corner all the way to the other corner. A slanted line is called a diagonal.
It looks like a staircase. And see? Every square on this diagonal is the same colour. That is true for every diagonal on the board. Each one is all light, or all dark.
Every square has its own name, just like every house has its own address. Let's find the name of this square.
First, look down to the letter at the bottom. This square is in the E file.
beats.speak: First, look down to the letter at the bottom. This square is in the letter E file.

beats.say: Next, look across to the number on the side. It is in rank four.
Letter first, then number. So the name of this square is e4!
Here is a white king. Which square is it standing on? It is in the C file, and in rank six.
So the king lives on c6. That is its address.
Quiz time! What is the name of this square? Find the letter at the bottom, then the number on the side. Pause the video and say it out loud.

quiz.why: Naming a square: the answer is g2.

beats.say: It is in the G file, and in rank two. So it is g2! Well done!
One more. Is this line a file, a rank, or a diagonal? Have a think.

quiz.why: Naming a kind of line: the d-file is a file.

beats.say: It goes straight up and down, so it is a file. It is the D file!
Now, here is how the armies stand when a game begins. White fills ranks one and two. Black fills ranks seven and eight.
Soon you will meet every one of these pieces, and learn how each one moves.
Great job! Now you know files, ranks, and diagonals, and you can name a square. Next time, we will meet the pawn. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Pawn
teaches: Each side has eight pawns.
A pawn moves straight forward one square.
On its first move a pawn may move two squares.
Forward is up the board for white and down the board for black.
A pawn never moves backward.
A pawn cannot move forward if a piece stands right in front of it; it cannot jump.
Pawns capture one square diagonally forward, never straight ahead.
A blocked pawn cannot walk forward, but it may still catch on the slant.
Most pieces are worth points; a pawn is worth one point.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to meet the smallest soldier in the chess army. It is called... the pawn!
Look at all these pawns! White has a row of pawns, and black has a row of pawns too.
Let's count the white pawns together. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight!
Eight pawns! Black has eight pawns too.
A pawn walks forward, one little step at a time.
Step. Step. Step!
But here is a secret. When a pawn moves for the very first time, it can take one step, or a giant step of two squares!
Big step! Two squares at once.
After that, the giant step is used up. Now it can only take one step again.
Step.
Black pawns walk forward too. But for black, forward is down the board, toward the white side.
White marches up. Black marches down. The two armies walk toward each other!
Can a pawn walk backward? No, never! Pawns are very brave. They only go forward.
And if something is standing right in front of a pawn, the pawn cannot walk forward. It cannot push it, and it cannot jump over it.
Now, look. Three black pawns are standing in front of our white pawn. Which ones can it catch? Let's find out!
Not the one straight ahead! A pawn walks straight, but it never catches straight.
A pawn catches on the slant, one step diagonally forward. So it can catch this one, or this one.
Gotcha!
Remember the pawn with something right in front of it? It cannot walk forward. But it may still catch on the slant! This black pawn is on the slant, so it can be caught.
Snap! The stuck pawn is not stuck any more.
Most chess pieces are worth some points. A pawn is worth one point. That is the smallest number.
But you have eight pawns. Eight pawns together are worth eight points. Little pawns are strong when they work as a team!
Quiz time! This white pawn has never moved. Where can it go? Pause the video, and point to the squares.
It can take one step, to here. Or, because it is its very first move, it can take a giant step of two, to here. Well done!
One more! Which black pawn can the white pawn catch? Have a think.
The one on the slant! The pawn straight ahead is safe, because pawns never catch straight.
Gotcha!
Great job! Now you know how the pawn walks, how it takes a giant step on its first move, and how it catches. Next time, we will play a fun pawn game. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Pawn Wars
teaches: Pawns start on rank 2 for white and rank 7 for black.
White always moves first; then the players take turns, one move each.

Game: Pawn Wars — only pawns, on their starting ranks; you win by getting a pawn to the far end, capturing all the other pawns, or leaving the other player with no move on their turn (that last rule is for this game only; real chess is different).
When you block a pawn, your own pawn cannot walk forward either, but it may still catch on the slant.
In a race, count the steps each pawn needs to see who gets there first.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Do you remember the brave little pawns? Today we will play a game with only pawns. It is called Pawn Wars!
Here is how to start. Put the white pawns on rank two, and the black pawns on rank seven. That is where pawns start in a real chess game too.
White always moves first. Then black moves. Then white again. You take turns, one move each.
White moves a pawn up the board. Then black moves a pawn. For black, forward is down the board.
Look! The black pawn is on the slant from the white pawn. Remember how pawns catch?
Gotcha! A pawn catches one step on the slant.
So how do you win Pawn Wars? There are three ways to win. Let's look at each one.
Way number one. Get one of your pawns all the way to the other end of the board.
White wants to reach the top. Black wants to reach the bottom. It is a race! And white goes first.
White steps. Black steps.
Now it is white's turn again. The white pawn needs just one more step, to this square at the end. Black cannot stop it.
Step! White gets to the far side first. In this game, the pawn simply stays there, and white wins the race!
Way number two. Catch all of the other player's pawns.
Black has only one pawn left. And it is on the slant from the white pawn!
Gotcha! Now black has no pawns at all. White wins!
Way number three is tricky. In this game, if it is your turn, and none of your pawns can move, you lose. Real chess has a different rule for that, and we will learn it later.
Look at the black pawn. A white pawn is standing right in front of it, so it cannot step forward. And there is nothing to catch on the slant.
White moves the other pawn. Now it is black's turn. But black cannot move at all. White wins!
Be careful with this one. When you block a pawn, your own pawn cannot walk forward any more either. It can still catch on the slant, if a black pawn comes there.
Quiz time! It is white's turn. Black has just one pawn left. Can white win right now? Pause the video and think.

quiz.why: Whether white wins depends on the Pawn Wars win rule (catch every enemy pawn); white wins with the catch d5xe6.

beats.say: Yes! The black pawn is on the slant, so the white pawn can catch it.
Gotcha! Black has no pawns left. White wins!
One more. It is white's turn. Which pawn will win the race to the end? Count the steps each pawn needs.

quiz.why: A race under the Pawn Wars rule (first pawn to the end wins): counting steps, white needs four and black two, so black wins.

beats.say: The white pawn needs four steps. The black pawn needs only two. So black will win, even though white goes first!
Step. Step. Step. Now it is black's turn. Black needs just one more step, to this square at the end, and white cannot stop it.
Step! The black pawn reaches the end first. Black wins the race!
Great job! Now you know how to play Pawn Wars. Ask a grown-up or a friend to play it with you. Next time, we will meet the rook. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Rook
teaches: The rook looks like a tower; some people call it a castle, but its name is the rook.
The rook moves in straight lines: up, down, left, or right, as far as it likes.
The rook can move backward.
The rook never moves diagonally.
In one move the rook goes in one direction only; it cannot turn a corner.
A rook cannot jump over pieces; it must stop before its own piece.
The rook captures the way it moves, landing on the piece's square and stopping there.
The rook catches the same way it moves; the pawn is different, because it walks straight but catches on the slant.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will meet a fast and strong piece. It looks like a tower. It is called... the rook!
Here is the rook. Some people call it a castle, because it looks like a castle tower. But its real chess name is the rook.
The rook moves in straight lines. Up. Down. Left. And right.
It can zoom a long way, or just one square. Nothing may stand in its path. Every green dot is a square it can reach!
Look at the rook's lines. They make a plus sign, like the plus sign in adding numbers.
Watch it zoom! Up. Across. Down. Whoosh! A rook can even go backward.
But the rook never moves on the slant. These squares are a no.
Here is another rule. In one move, the rook picks one direction and goes straight. It cannot turn a corner. So how can it get to this square?
Up first. Then across. It takes two moves.
What if its own pawn is in the way? The rook must stop before it. A rook cannot jump over pieces.
Now, how does the rook catch? That is easy. It catches the same way it moves.
It slides straight to the black pawn and takes its square. But then it must stop. It cannot keep going past.
Gotcha! The black pawn is gone, and the rook stays right there.
So the rook catches the same way it moves, straight along a line. The pawn is different. It walks straight, but it catches on the slant.
Quiz time! Which black pawns can the rook catch? Pause the video, and point to them.
This one, straight up. And this one, straight across. But not the middle one. It is on the slant, and rooks only go straight.
Gotcha!
One more. Can the rook catch the black pawn right now, in one move? Have a think.
No, not in one move! The rook's own pawn is standing in the way, and in a normal move a rook cannot jump over a piece.
Great job! Now you know the rook moves in straight lines, as far as it likes, and catches the way it moves. Next time, we will play rook games. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Rampant Rooks
teaches: Game: Pawn Hunt (rooks) — each player has one rook in opposite corners and eight pawns placed anywhere that never move; the first to capture all the other player's pawns wins; in this game, a side that cannot move on its turn loses, so losing your rook loses the game.
A rook can capture the other rook: two rooks on a clear line can capture each other, so whoever moves first wins it.

Game: Rooks and Pawns — rooks in the corners and pawns on their starting ranks; win by capturing every enemy piece, or by getting a pawn to the far end where it is safe; in this game, a side that cannot move on its turn loses.
A pawn at the far end is safe only if the other side cannot capture it in one move.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Rampant means wild and full of energy. Today we will play two games, to practise zooming the rooks around.
The first game is called Pawn Hunt.
Each player gets one rook. The two rooks start in opposite corners of the board.
Then each player puts their eight pawns on the board, anywhere they like. In this game, the pawns never move. Only the rooks move!
The goal is to catch all of the other player's pawns, before they catch all of yours. And in this game, if it is your turn and you cannot move at all, you lose.
White goes first. The rook slides across, and now it is aiming at a black pawn.
Black slides too, and now it is aiming at a white pawn.
White catches first. Gotcha!
And black catches back. Gotcha! The hunt goes on.
Can a rook catch the other rook? Yes, it can! Look. These two rooks are on the same file, with nothing between them.
If your rook can catch their rook, then their rook can catch yours too. So whoever moves first wins it!
If it is white's turn, gotcha! In Pawn Hunt the pawns never move, so a side with no rook cannot move at all. That side loses! So be careful where you put your rook.
Here is the second game. This time, the pawns can move too.
Put both rooks in the corners, and all the pawns on their starting ranks, just like at the start of a real game.
You win if you catch every one of the other player's pieces.
Or, in this game, you win if one of your pawns reaches the other end of the board, and it is safe there. That is different from Pawn Wars, where reaching the end wins straight away.
And one more rule, just for this game. If it is your turn and you cannot move at all, you lose. Just like in Pawn Wars!
What does safe mean? Look. A white pawn just reached the end. But black gets one more turn, to try to catch it.
Oh no! The black rook can slide straight across to it.
Gotcha! That pawn was not safe, so it does not win.
Now another pawn reaches the end. Can the black rook catch it, in just one move?
No! The rook can slide across, or slide up, but it cannot land on the pawn in one move. The pawn is safe. White wins!
Quiz time! We are playing Pawn Hunt. Which black pawns can the white rook catch right now? Pause the video and point.
This one, straight up. And this one, straight across. The middle pawn is on the slant, so it is safe.
One more. Now we are playing Rooks and Pawns. The white pawn just reached the end. Black gets one move. Is the pawn safe? Have a think.
It is safe! The rook can go up, or go across, but it cannot reach the pawn in one move. White wins!
Great job! Now you know two rook games. Ask a grown-up or a friend to play them with you. Next time, we will meet the bishop. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Bishop
teaches: The bishop wears a tall, pointy hat with a little cut in it.
The bishop moves on diagonals, as far as it likes, if nothing is in the way.
The bishop can move backward, like the rook; the pawn never can.
A bishop always stays on squares of the colour it starts on.
Each army has two bishops: one starts on a dark square, one on a light square.
An army's two bishops never share a square: a square one of them can visit, the other one can never visit.
The bishop captures the way it moves.
A bishop cannot jump over pieces.
A bishop can only ever visit half of the squares on the board.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will meet a piece that loves to travel on the slant. It is called... the bishop!
Here is the bishop. Look at its head. It wears a tall, pointy hat with a little cut in it.
The bishop moves on diagonals. Remember? A diagonal is a slanted line of squares, like a staircase.
It can go as far as it likes along a diagonal, as long as nothing is in the way. It can go to any of these squares!
Look at the bishop's lines. They make a big X. The rook makes a plus, and the bishop makes an X!
Whoosh! Up the slant. And back down again. Did you see? The bishop can go backward.
The rook can go backward too. But the pawn never can. Pawns only go forward.
Now look at the square the bishop is standing on. It is a dark square. And every square on its diagonals is dark too.
So this bishop will always stay on dark squares. Forever and ever!
Each army has two bishops. At the start of the game, one stands on a dark square, and one stands on a light square.
The dark square bishop only visits dark squares. The light square bishop only visits light squares.
So these two bishops never share a square. Any square one of them can visit, the other one never can.
The bishop catches the same way it moves. It slides along the slant, and takes the black pawn's square.
Gotcha!
And just like the rook, a bishop cannot jump. Here its own pawn blocks the way, so it must stop before it.
Now look. Two black pawns are standing right next to the bishop. Can the bishop catch them?
No! They are on light squares, and this bishop only goes on dark squares. They are safe from it.
So the bishop is fast, and it can go backward. But it can only ever visit half of the squares on the board.
Quiz time! Which black pawn can the bishop catch? Pause the video, and point to it.
This one, along the slant! The other pawn is straight ahead, and a bishop never moves straight.
Gotcha!
One more. This bishop is on a dark square. The black pawn is on a light square. If the pawn stays right there, could the bishop ever catch it, even with lots of moves?

quiz.why: Asks about a pawn that stays on its light square: a bishop keeps its square colour, so the dark-square bishop can never reach that square. (If the pawn steps to a dark square, it can be caught; the answer beat says so.)

beats.say: Not while the pawn stays there! A dark square bishop stays on dark squares. A pawn on a light square is safe from it.
Great job! Now you know the bishop moves on diagonals, as far as it likes, and always stays on its own colour. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Busy Bishops
teaches: White bishops start on c1 and f1; black bishops start on c8 and f8.

Game: Pawn Hunt (bishops) — each side has two bishops on their starting squares and eight pawns placed anywhere that never move; the first to capture all the other side's pawns wins; in this game, a side that cannot move on its turn loses, so losing both bishops loses the game.
Bishops can capture each other, so don't put yours where the other bishop can get it.
A bishop stuck behind its own pawns comes out when a pawn moves to open the way.

Game: Mini Game — bishops and pawns on their starting squares, pawns move and capture as normal; win by capturing every enemy piece or by getting a pawn to the far end where nobody can capture it; in this game, a side that cannot move on its turn loses.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today our bishops are going to be very busy. We are going to play some bishop games!
First, let's remember how the bishop moves. It slides on the slant, as far as it likes.
Whoosh! Whoosh!
At the start of a game, the white bishops stand here, on c1 and f1.
And the black bishops stand up here, on c8 and f8. Right next to where the knights will go.
Look at this white bishop. It starts on a dark square, so it will always stay on dark squares.
Its brother starts on a light square, so it always stays on light squares. Two bishops, two colours!
Our first game is called Pawn Hunt. Each side has two bishops, standing on their starting squares.
Each side also has eight pawns. You can put your pawns anywhere you like. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight.
Here is the big rule. In Pawn Hunt, the pawns never move. They stand still, like statues. Only the bishops move.

Take turns. Try to catch the other side's pawns with your bishops. Whoever catches all the other pawns first is the winner! And in this game, just like in the rook game, if it is your turn and you cannot move at all, you lose.
Be careful! Bishops can catch each other too. So don't put your bishop where the other bishop can get it. If both of your bishops get caught, you cannot move at all, and you lose!
Quiz time! White always goes first. Can you find a black pawn that a white bishop can catch right now?
This one! The bishop on c1 can slide up the slant and catch it.
Gotcha!
Now black slides a bishop out. Uh oh! It is looking at a white pawn. The hunt is on!
Here is another game. The bishops stand on their starting squares, and all the pawns stand on their starting rows.
This time, the pawns can move too! Pawns walk and catch, just like in a real game.
But look. The bishops are stuck behind their own pawns. A bishop cannot jump over anything.
So we move a pawn, to open a door.
Now this bishop has a long slant to slide along. It is ready to come out!
Black opens a door too. Now both armies have a busy bishop ready to go.

To win, catch every piece on the other side. Or walk one of your pawns all the way to the far end, where nobody can catch it. And in this game, if it is your turn and you cannot move at all, you lose.
One more! Which black pawns can this white bishop catch? Have a think.
These two, on the slant! The pawn straight ahead is safe, because a bishop never moves straight.
Gotcha!
Great job! Now you can play Pawn Hunt and the mini game with your bishops. Next time, we will meet the strongest piece of all, the queen. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Queen
teaches: The queen is the strongest piece.
The queen moves straight like a rook and diagonally like a bishop: rook plus bishop.
The queen can go as far as she likes in one move.
From the middle of an empty board the queen reaches 27 squares, more than any other piece.
The queen cannot jump over pieces.
The queen captures by landing on the enemy piece's square.
The queen is worth nine points.
Take good care of your queen; don't let it be captured.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to meet the strongest piece in the whole chess army. It is the queen!
Here she is. The queen is super fast, and she can go in lots of different directions.
She can slide straight. Up, down, and side to side, just like a rook.
She can also slide on the slant, just like a bishop.
Put the rook and the bishop together, and you get the queen! Forward, backward, sideways, and on the slant.
And she can go as far as she likes, in one move. Let's watch her zoom.
Zoom! Zoom! Zoom!
When the queen stands in the middle of an empty board, look at all the squares she can reach!
Twenty seven squares! That is almost half of the whole board. No other piece can reach so many.
But even the queen cannot jump over pieces. Her own pawn is in the way, so she cannot go past it.
If an enemy piece is on her path, she can catch it. She lands right on its square.
Gotcha!
Remember, most pieces are worth some points. A pawn is worth one point. The queen is worth nine points!
She is so strong that we must take good care of her. Don't let the other side catch your queen!
Quiz time! There are four black pieces. The queen can catch three of them. Which one is safe? Pause the video and point.
The horse-shaped piece is safe! We will meet it soon. It is not on a straight line or a slant from the queen. She can catch all the others.
One more! Right now, in one move, can the queen catch the black rook, or the black bishop? Have a think.
Her own pawn blocks the way to the rook. But the slant to the bishop is wide open!
Zoom! Gotcha! And the black rook cannot reach her there, so the queen is safe.
Great job! Now you know the queen moves like a rook and a bishop together. Next time, we will play a fun game with the queen. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Quirky Queens
teaches: Each queen starts in the middle of her back row, on the d file (d1 and d8).
The queen starts on her own colour: the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark square.

Game: Queen Chase — one black queen against eight white pawns, white first; in this game the pawns win if one reaches the far end and cannot be captured straight away, or if a pawn captures the queen; the queen wins by capturing all eight; as in Pawn Wars, a side that cannot move on its turn loses (a rule of this game, not of real chess).
Never land your queen where a pawn can capture it; look before you land.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will find out where the queen stands, and then we will play a chasing game with her!
At the start of a game, each queen stands in the middle of her back row. White here, and black up here.
Here is a trick to remember. Look at the white queen. She stands on a light square.
Now look at the black queen. She stands on a dark square.
The white queen on a light square. The black queen on a dark square. The queen always starts on her own colour!
Both queens stand on the same up and down line. This line is called the d file.
Now let's play a game called Queen Chase. Black has just one queen. White has eight pawns.
The pawns want to run all the way to the other end of the board.
The queen wants to catch every single pawn before any of them gets there.
In this game, a pawn at the end must also be safe. If a pawn reaches the end, and the queen cannot catch it straight away, the pawns win.

If the queen catches all eight pawns, the queen wins! But if a pawn catches the queen, the pawns win. And just like in Pawn Wars, if it is your turn and you cannot move at all, you lose. That is a rule of this game, not of real chess. White always goes first.
White pushes a pawn. But look! The queen can zoom straight down the line to a pawn.
Gotcha! One pawn caught.
But the queen must be careful too. Pawns catch on the slant. If a pawn catches the queen, the pawns win the game! So never stop where a pawn can catch her.
Oh no! The pawn caught the queen, so the pawns win. Always look before you land.
Quiz time! The queen can catch two pawns. One is a trap! Which pawn is safe to catch? Pause the video and think.

quiz.why: The queen can catch on b4 or g6, but b4 is guarded by the pawn on a3, so only g6 is a safe catch.

beats.say: Not this one! If the queen lands here, the pawn behind it can catch her on the slant.
This one is safe. Nobody can catch the queen over here.
Gotcha!
One more! This white pawn is just one step from the end. It is black's turn. Can the queen catch it right now? Have a think.
Yes! The queen zooms all the way up the slant and catches it.
Gotcha! The queen saves the day.
Great job! Now you know the queen starts on her own colour, and you can play Queen Chase. Next time, we will meet the knight. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Knight
teaches: The knight looks like a horse; each side has two knights.
The knight moves in an L shape: two squares straight, then one square to the side.
The same L can also be made one square to the side, then two squares straight.
A knight in the middle of the board can reach eight squares.
Every knight move takes it to a square of the other colour.
The knight can jump over other pieces; no other piece can.
A knight captures only a piece on the square where it lands, never the pieces it jumps over.
A knight in the corner can reach only two squares, so knights are happiest in the middle.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to meet the trickiest piece on the board. It is the knight!
The knight looks like a horse. White has two knights. One, two. Black has two knights too.
A knight is a brave soldier who rides on a horse. That is why the piece has a horse's head.
The knight moves in a very special way. Its move makes a shape like the letter L.
Two steps straight, then one step to the side. Like this.
Hop! It lands right here.
Here is another way to see it. One step to the side, then two steps straight. Same L, same square!
Hop!
When the knight stands in the middle, it can hop to all of these squares. Each one is at the end of an L.
Let's put a pawn on every one. Count with me. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!
Eight squares, in a ring all the way around the knight.
Here is a secret. Look at the square the knight is standing on. It is a light square.
Now look at the squares it can hop to. They are all dark squares!
Every time the knight hops, it changes colour. Light, dark, light, dark.
The knight has a super power that no other piece has. It can jump over other pieces!
Look. Pieces are all around it. But the knight can still hop out, to any of these eight squares.
Boing! Right over the top.
Does the knight catch the pieces it jumps over? Let's see. This knight will hop over these two pawns.
The pawns are still there! The knight only catches a piece on the square where it lands. Here, that was the bishop.
Quiz time! This black knight can catch two white pieces. Which ones? Look for the L. Pause the video and point.
The two rooks! The bishop and the pawn are right next to the knight, but they are not at the end of an L.
Gotcha!
One more! This knight is stuck in the corner. How many squares can it hop to? Have a think.
Only two! In the middle, a knight has eight squares. In the corner, just two. Knights are happiest in the middle.
Great job! Now you know the knight hops in an L, changes colour, and jumps over pieces. Next time, we will play knight games. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Hungry Horses
teaches: Game: Hungry Horse — each side has just one knight, placed inside the enemy army, and the other pieces stand on their starting squares; only the two knights move, and whoever captures all the other side's pieces first wins; in this game, a side whose knight is captured, or cannot move on its turn, loses.
Game: Knight Hop — a lone knight hops to each corner of the board in turn and back home; in this game, it may never land on a pawn or on a square a pawn guards.
Term: guard — a piece guards a square if it could capture there.
A pawn guards the two squares diagonally in front of it; black pawns guard downward.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! The knight is the trickiest piece, so it needs lots of practice. Today we will play two knight games!
The first game is called Hungry Horse. Almost all the pieces we know stand on their starting squares. But each side has just one knight.
And look up here! The white knight has sneaked right into the middle of the black army.
And the black knight has sneaked into the white army, down here.
In this game, only these two knights can move. Everything else stands still.

The knights are hungry for pieces! Each knight tries to catch the other side's pieces. Whoever catches all of them first is the winner. And in this game, if your one knight gets caught, or it has no move on your turn, you lose.
Quiz time! White goes first. Which black pieces can the hungry white knight catch right now? Pause the video and point.
These two pawns! Each one is at the end of an L.
Gotcha! The knight catches a pawn.
Now it is black's turn. The black knight catches a pawn too.
Look where the white knight is now. It can reach a big black rook!
Gotcha! That rook is caught.
But the black knight copies, and catches a white rook. What a hungry game!
The second game is called Knight Hop. You can play it all by yourself. Our knight starts in this corner.
It must hop to every corner of the board, one by one. First the other bottom corner, then the top corner above it, then the last top corner, and then back home.
But watch out! There are black pawns in the way. In this game, the knight must never land on a pawn.
And in this game, it must never land where a pawn could catch it. Black pawns catch on the slant, down the board. So this pawn guards these two squares.
Here are all the squares the pawns guard. In this game, the knight may not land on any of them.
Let's hop to the first corner together. Watch carefully.
Hop. Hop. Hop. Hop. And hop! We made it to the corner in five hops!
Now it is your turn. Can you hop to the next corner, then the next, and then all the way home?
One more quiz! Which two squares does this black pawn guard? Remember, black pawns go down the board. Have a think.

quiz.why: Asks which squares a pawn guards (its two slant squares, both empty), not a move or capture

beats.say: These two, on the slant below it! In this game, a knight must not land on either one.
Great job! Now you can play Hungry Horse with a friend, and Knight Hop all by yourself. Next time, we will meet the most important piece of all, the king. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The King
teaches: Each side has exactly one king.
If your king is attacked and nothing can save him, you lose the game.
The king moves one square in any direction: straight or diagonally.
Nobody may ever capture a king, so the king may never move to a square an enemy piece attacks.
If your king is in danger, you must get him out of danger at once.
The two kings may never stand on neighbouring squares.
The king's crown has a little cross on top, which tells him apart from the queen.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to meet the most important piece of all. It is the king!
Each side has just one king. Here is the white king, and here is the black king.
The king is so important that if your king is attacked and nothing can save him, you lose the game. So we must always keep him safe.
The king can move in any direction. Up, down, side to side, and on the slant.
But he is a slow old king. He can only take one step at a time.
Step. Step. Step.
Here is a very important rule. Nobody is ever allowed to catch a king. So the king must never step onto a square where an enemy could catch him.
And if your king is ever in danger, you must get him out of danger straight away.
Look at this white king. He wants to take a step. But the black queen and the black rook are watching.
The rook watches this whole line. If the king stepped here, here, or here, the rook could catch him.
And the queen watches these squares. The king cannot go there either.
Only one square is safe. Nobody is watching it. Can you find it?
This one! Nobody is watching it.
Step! Safe and sound.
One more rule. The two kings may never stand next to each other. There must always be at least one square between them.
So the white king cannot step up to any of these squares. They are too close to the other king.
How can you tell the king from the queen? Look at the very top. The king wears a crown with a little cross on it.
Quiz time! The black rook watches this whole row. Where can the white king step safely? Pause the video and point.
Not up, because the rook is watching. But he can step sideways, to this square or this one. Well done!
One more! Can the white king step up to this square? Have a think.

quiz.why: Yes/no rule question: may a king step next to the other king (answer: no)

beats.say: No! Then the two kings would be standing next to each other. That is never allowed.
Great job! Now you know the king takes one step at a time, and never steps into danger. Next time, we will play a game to keep the king safe. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Mine Alert
teaches: Game: Mine Alert — the black pieces are mines, and the white king walks one step at a time to a target square without stepping on a mine or on any square a mine guards.
A piece is dangerous not only on its own square but on every square it guards.
Term: danger square — a square an enemy piece guards, so it could catch the king there.
A pawn guards only the two squares on the slant in front of it, never the square straight ahead.
To plan a king walk, mark the danger squares first, then find a path of safe single steps around them.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to play a brave little game for the king. It is called... Mine Alert!
Here is our white king. Do you remember how the king walks?
The king takes one small step at a time. He can step up, down, sideways, or on the slant. Just one step!
In Mine Alert, the black pieces are mines. Boom! Our king must never step on a mine.
But here is the tricky part. A mine also guards squares. It guards every square where it could catch our king. This rook mine guards all of these squares.
A square that a mine guards is called a danger square. So the king must not step on a mine, and not on a square with a cross either.
Pawn mines are different. A black pawn catches on the slant, down the board. So it guards only these two squares.
The square straight in front of the pawn is not a danger square. The pawn cannot catch there, so the king may step on it.
Let's try one together. Our king wants to walk all the way up to this square, at the top of the board.
There is a bishop mine in the middle. A bishop goes on the slants, so these slanty squares are danger squares.
First, the king walks straight up. Step. Step. Step!
Oh! The mine is right in front of him. He cannot step on it. He must walk around it.
Step around this way. And step back to the middle. No danger squares there!
Step, and step. He made it! The king is safe.
Quiz time! Look at the rook mine over on the side. Can our king step up to this square? Have a think.

quiz.why: Yes/no question: can the king step onto one square the rook guards (answer: no)

beats.say: No, he can't! The rook mine reaches all along that row. Those squares are danger squares.
But the squares with a dot are safe. The king can step there. Well done!
Now a big puzzle! Look at all these mines. Our white king starts down here. He wants to reach this square at the very top.
Remember, one step at a time, and no danger squares. Can you find a safe path? Pause the video and trace it with your finger.

quiz.why: Trace a multi-step safe path for the king; a path is not one move

beats.say: Let's find it together. Look, the knight and the rook are guarding the squares near the start. So the king can't go there.
So first, he sneaks up on the slant, and then over this way.
Now he climbs the slant. Step, and step. Nobody guards the squares he steps on.
Step, and step. He is tiptoeing right past the mines!
And one last step. Hooray! The king made it to the top without a single boom!
Great job! The king must never step on a mine, or on a square a mine guards. You can make your own Mine Alert puzzles at home. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Check and Checkmate
teaches: The king is never taken off the board; instead we attack him so that nothing can save him.
Term: check — the king is attacked.
Every piece except the king can give check, even a pawn.
A king may not capture a guarded piece, because he would be stepping into danger.
A king in check must get out of check at once.
There are three ways out of check, remembered as A, B, C.
A is for avoid: the king moves to a safe square.
B is for block: put one of your own pieces between the attacker and your king.
C is for capture: take the piece giving check, with any of your pieces.
Term: checkmate — the king is in check and cannot avoid, block, or capture; the game is over.
A check is not checkmate if the king can capture an unguarded attacker.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we learn the most exciting thing in chess. How to attack the king!
Here is a funny thing. In chess, we never take the king off the board. Never ever!
Instead, we try to attack him so that nothing can save him. Let's find out how.
Look! The white queen is attacking the black king. When a king is attacked, we call it check!
Now the black rook is attacking the white king. Check!
The white bishop zooms along the slant. Check!
The black knight hops. Check!
Even a little pawn can give check! This white pawn is attacking the black king on the slant.
Hmm. Can the black king just catch that pawn? Have a think.
No! The other pawn is guarding it. A king can never step into danger, so he can't take that pawn.
So who can't give check? The king! Two kings may never stand side by side. Neither king may step on these squares in the middle.
When your king is in check, you can't ignore it. You must get him out of check right away!
There are three ways to get out of check. They are easy to remember, because they go A, B, C!
A is for avoid. The king runs away to a safe square. Here, this is the only safe square.
Run away! Now the king is safe.
B is for block. Put one of your own pieces in the way, between the attacker and your king.
The black rook zooms up and stands in the way. Now the queen can't reach the king!
C is for capture. Take the piece that is giving check! You can use any of your pieces to do it.
Look at this sneaky black bishop, way down near the corner. It can slide up the slant.
Gotcha! The queen is gone, so the check is gone too. Here, capturing is the best way out, because black wins the white queen!
So remember. Avoid. Block. Capture. Always look for all three!
But what if the king can't do any of them? Look. The black king is in check. Let's try our A, B, C.
A. Can he run away? No. The queen guards every empty square around him.
B. Can anyone block? No. The queen is right next to him. There is no room in between.
C. Can the king capture the queen? No! The white king is guarding her.
He is attacked, and nothing can save him: he can't run, block, or capture. This is called checkmate! The game is over, and White wins.
Quiz time! Here is our check again. Can you remember the three ways to get out of check? Say them out loud!

quiz.why: Naming the three ways out of check

beats.say: Avoid, by running away. Block, by getting in the way. And capture, by taking the attacker. Well done!
One more! The black king is in check. But this time, the white king is far away. Is it checkmate? Have a think.
No! Nobody is guarding the queen. So the black king can capture her.
Gotcha! Not checkmate after all.
Great job! Check means the king is attacked. Checkmate means he is attacked, nothing can save him, and the game is over. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Getting Your King Safe
teaches: Term: castling — a special move of the king and a rook together.
Castling moves two pieces, the king and a rook, in one turn.
When castling, the king moves two squares toward the rook.
The rook then hops over the king to the square right beside him; this rook hop is the one exception to the rule that only the knight jumps over pieces.
Castling rule one: every square between the king and the rook must be empty.
Castling rule two: the king and that rook must never have moved.
These are only some of the castling rules; the rest come in When You Can or Can't Castle.
Term: kingside — the half of the board where the king stands at the start (files e to h); castling there is castling kingside.
Term: queenside — the half of the board where the queen stands at the start (files a to d); castling there is castling queenside.
Castling moves the king toward the side of the board, near the corner, behind a wall of pawns, where he is safe.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! If your king is attacked and nothing can save him, the game is over. So today we learn a special move that tucks him away safely.
Look at the king and the rook. They are good friends. And together, they can do a special dance.
This dance is called castling. Can you say castling? Castling!
Castling is a very special move. It lets you do three things that are normally not allowed.
Number one. You move two pieces, the king and the rook, in just one turn.
Number two. The king takes two steps, instead of just one.
Number three. The rook hops over the king, to his other side. Remember, only the knight jumps over pieces. But when the rook hops over the king in castling, that is the one exception!
Watch the dance. The king steps two squares toward the rook. Then the rook hops over and lands right next to him!
But castling has rules. Here are some of them. Rule one: the squares between the king and the rook must be empty. Here, a bishop is in the way. No castling yet!
Rule two: the king and the rook must never have moved before. Not even one tiny step! There are a few more rules. We will learn them in the episode When You Can or Can't Castle.
Now look. Here, both sides are allowed to castle. Nothing is in the way, nobody has moved yet, and the other rules say yes too.
White castles on this side. The king goes two steps, and the rook hops over.
At the start of a game, the king stands on this half of the board. So this half is called the kingside, and White just castled kingside.
Black castles on the other side. Look, all the squares between the black king and rook are empty.
The king goes two steps toward the rook. And the rook hops over to stand beside him.
At the start of a game, the queen stands on this half of the board. So this half is called the queenside, and Black just castled queenside.
Why do we castle? Because it moves the king over to the side, near the corner, behind a wall of pawns. Cozy and safe!
But this black king has no wall in front of him. He is out in the open. That is where the big fights happen.
Quiz time! White wants to castle. Which square will the king land on? Point to it!

quiz.why: Rule question: which square the king lands on when castling

beats.say: Right here! Two steps toward the rook.
And the rook hops over and lands beside him. Well done!
One more! Can White castle here? Have a think.
No! The knight is standing in the way. The squares between them must be empty.
Let's move the knight out of the way. Hop!
Now the path is clear. Castle!
Great job! Castling is the dance of the king and the rook. It helps keep your king safe. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Setting Up the Board Correctly
teaches: Before setting up, make sure the board is the right way round: the corner square on your right must be light ("Light on the right!").
The rooks go in the four corners.
Each knight goes right next to a rook.
The queen goes on her own colour: the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark square.
The king goes right next to his queen, on the other middle square.
The bishops fill the last two back-row squares, one on each side of the king and queen.
The back row reads rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, bishop, knight, rook.
The pawns stand in a row right in front of the big pieces.
Each side starts with sixteen pieces.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Before we can play, we have to put all the pieces in the right places. Let's learn how!
Here is an empty chess board. But wait! First we must make sure that it is the right way round.
Look at the corner on your right, closest to you. That corner square must be a light square.
Here is a little rhyme to help you. Light on the right! Say it with me. Light on the right!
Now the pieces. The rooks look like little castle towers. So they stand in the four corners, like towers on a castle wall.
One, two, three, four rooks. One in every corner!
Next come the horses, the knights. Each knight stands right next to a rook, to help guard the castle.
Now the king and queen go in the middle. But which one goes where? Here is the trick.
The queen likes to match. So the white queen sits on a light square, and the black queen sits on a dark square.
And the king? He sits right next to his queen, on the other middle square.
Only two empty squares left in each row. The bishops go there, one on each side of the king and queen.
Look! The whole back row is full. Rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, bishop, knight, rook.
Last of all, the pawns. They stand in a line, right in front of the big pieces, like a wall.
Let's count the white pieces. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!
Sixteen pieces! And black has sixteen pieces too. The board is ready to play.
Quiz time! Oh no, the queens are missing! Where does the white queen go? Point to her square.

quiz.why: Setting-up rule: where the white queen starts

beats.say: Right here, on the light square. The queen matches her colour!
And the black queen goes on the dark square, across from her. Well done!
One more! Before you put any pieces on the board, what must you make sure of? Can you say the rhyme?

quiz.why: Naming the board-orientation rhyme

beats.say: Light on the right! The corner square on your right must be light. Hooray!
Great job! Rooks in the corners, then knights, then the queen on her colour, the king, the bishops, and the pawns. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Why We Should Castle
teaches: At the start of the game both kings stand in the middle of their back row.
The middle of the board is where the pieces rush to fight.
To castle, first move the pieces between the king and the rook out of the way.
Castling moves the king away from the busy middle, over toward the corner.
After castling, the three pawns in front of the king form a wall that keeps him safe.
A king left in the middle is in danger when the fighting starts there.
After castling, leave the wall pawns at home; if they move, enemies can sneak in through the holes.
Castle early.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! You know how to castle. Today we find out why castling is such a good idea.
At the start of the game, both kings sit right in the middle of their back row.
But the middle of the board is where all the action happens. The pieces rush there to fight.
Look, the pawns march out, and the knights jump out.
Now the bishops slide out too. The space between the white king and rook is empty!
So White castles. The king hurries away from the busy middle, over toward the corner.
And look who is standing in front of him. Three pawns! They are like a wall that keeps the king safe.
Here is another game. Look at the two kings. Which one would you rather be?
The white king has castled. He is tucked away near the corner, behind his pawn wall.
The black king is still standing in the middle, right where the fighting is.
Now White pushes a pawn into the middle. It attacks two black pieces at once! The fight is starting, right in front of the black king.
And the white king? He is far away from all that trouble. That is why we castle!
Here is a top tip. After you castle, leave these three pawns at home. They are the king's wall.
Uh oh. If those pawns walk away, there are holes in the wall. Now enemies can sneak in to attack the king.
Quiz time! Look at the two kings again. Which king is safer, the white one or the black one?

quiz.why: Judgement: which king is safer

beats.say: The white king! He castled, and he is hiding behind his pawns. Well done!
One more! How many pawns are in the white king's wall? Count them with me.

quiz.why: Counting the pawns in the king's wall

beats.say: One, two, three! Three brave pawns, making a wall in front of the king.
Great job! Castle early, to get your king out of the busy middle. And keep his pawn wall in place. Bye bye!

lessons.title: When You Can or Can't Castle
teaches: Once the king has moved, he can never castle in that game, even if he steps back home.
You may not castle while your king is in check.
You may not castle if the king would land on a square where he would be in check.
You may not castle through check: the square the king passes over must not be attacked.
An enemy attacking squares on the other side of the board does not stop castling.
Castle early, before there is any danger.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Castling is a great way to keep your king safe. But sometimes, castling is not allowed. Let's find out when.
First, a reminder. The squares between the king and the rook must be empty.
And the king and rook must never have moved. Look, the king takes a step.
Now he steps back home. Can he castle now? No! He already moved, so no castling for this king, ever.
Those were rule one and rule two. Now here are three more rules: rule three, four and five. They are all about keeping the king out of danger.
Rule three. You can't castle when your king is in check. Look, the black bishop is attacking the white king.
So the king can't castle this way, and he can't castle that way. He has to deal with the check first.
Nobody can block, and nobody can capture the bishop. So the king must step away himself, to one of these safe squares.
He is safe now. But he has moved, so he can never castle in this game. Oh well!
Rule four. The king may not land where he would be in check. White wants to castle here. The king would end up on this square.
But look! The black bishop is watching that square. If the king landed there, he would be in check. So no castling!
Rule five. You can't castle through check. When the king castles, he walks over this square, and lands on this one.
The landing square is safe. But the black rook is watching the square he walks over. He can't walk through danger!
So remember. Not in check. Not into check. Not through check.
Quiz time! White wants to castle. Look at the black bishop. Can White castle? Have a think.
No! The bishop is watching the square the king walks over. That would be castling through check.
One more! Now there is a black rook. Can White castle this time?
Yes! The rook is watching a square over on the other side. The king is not in check, and his path is safe.
So, castle! Well done!
Great job! A good tip is to castle early in the game, before there is any danger. Then your king is much safer. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Pawn Magic
teaches: A pawn moves only forward, never backward.
Term: promotion — a pawn that reaches the last row turns into a new piece.
White's last row is the top row; Black's last row is the bottom row.
On promotion you choose a queen, rook, bishop, or knight; never a king, and the pawn may not stay a pawn.
The pawn is taken off and the new piece is put on that same square.
Usually choose a queen, the strongest piece; a knight is sometimes a clever surprise.
A pawn can also promote by capturing diagonally onto the last row.
The new piece works at once: it can even give check on the very move it appears.
Term: en passant — when an enemy pawn steps two squares and lands right beside your pawn, your pawn may capture it diagonally as if it had moved only one square.
En passant must be done on the very next move, or the chance is gone.
Only a pawn can capture en passant.

beats.say: Hello again, chess friends! Do you remember the little pawn? Today we will find out that pawns can do magic!
Here is a white pawn. It walks forward, one step at a time. It can never, ever walk backward.
Step. Step. On and on it goes.
Look at this row, right at the top. It is the very last row, the far side of the board. What happens when a pawn gets there?
One more step. Almost there!
Ta-da! Magic! The pawn reached the last row, and it turned into a queen!
This magic has a special name. It is called promotion. Promotion means you get a big upgrade, because you did a great job.
When your pawn gets to the last row, you choose what it turns into. A queen. A rook. A bishop. Or a knight.
You take the pawn off the board, and you put your new piece on that very same square.
Can the pawn turn into a king? No! You only ever have one king. And the pawn cannot stay a pawn either. It must change.
Most of the time, we pick the queen, because she is the strongest piece of all. Sometimes a knight is a clever surprise, but the queen is usually best.
Black pawns can do magic too. For black, the last row is down at the bottom of the board.
Step, and step. Ta-da! A black queen!
A pawn can also reach the last row by catching something on the slant. Watch this pawn catch the rook.
Gotcha! And because it landed on the last row, it turns into a queen at the same time. Double magic!
Here is one more surprise. The new piece gets to work straight away, on the very same move. Watch this pawn.
Ta-da! The brand new queen looks along the row, and she is already attacking the black king. Check!
Quiz time! Which white pawn is ready to do magic on its very next step? Pause the video and point to it.

quiz.why: Which pawn is one step from promoting; a choice of piece, not a move

beats.say: This one! It is only one step away from the last row.
Step. Ta-da! A brand new queen. Well done!
Now here is one more pawn trick. It is a tricky one, so do not worry if it feels hard. You can learn it again when you are bigger.
Look at this white pawn. It has marched three steps from home, to just past the middle of the board.
Now this black pawn is still at home. It has not moved yet. So it may take a giant step of two squares.
There it goes, a giant step of two squares, down the board. Remember, forward for black is down. Now it stands right next to the white pawn. It is trying to sneak past!
But the white pawn can still catch it! It catches on the slant, as if the black pawn had only taken one step.
Gotcha! The black pawn comes off the board. This trick is called en passant.
Remember, you must do it right away, on your very next move. If you wait, the chance is gone. And only a pawn can catch a pawn this way.
Great job! Now you know pawn magic. A pawn that reaches the last row gets promoted. Next time, we will find out how many points the pieces are worth. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Scoring Points
teaches: Some pieces are stronger than others; most pieces get a points score, and the king gets none.
Points do not win the game; you still win by checkmate.
The pawn is worth one point.
The knight is worth three points, and the bishop is worth three points too.
Three points is the same as three pawns.
The rook is worth five points.
The queen is worth nine points.
The king has no points, because he is never taken off the board.
Never give away your queen just to catch a pawn.
Add up the points of the pieces you caught to see who is ahead.
More pieces does not always mean more points.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Some chess pieces are stronger than others. Today most pieces get a score. A big score means a strong piece. The king is special, and you will see why.
Points do not win the game. You still win by checkmate, when the king is attacked and nothing can save him. But points help you see who is doing better.
Let's start with the smallest. The pawn is worth one point.
The knight, the jumpy horse, is worth three points.
The bishop is worth three points too. So a knight and a bishop are worth the same.
Three points is the same as three pawns. One. Two. Three.
Now the rook, the castle tower. The rook is worth five points.
That is as much as five pawns. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.
And the queen, the strongest piece of all, is worth nine points!
Nine pawns! One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Wow!
What about the king? The king never gets caught and taken off the board. So we do not give him any points.
The king has no score at all. He is too precious! If your king is attacked and nothing can save him, the game ends.
Let's say them all again. Pawn, one. Knight, three. Bishop, three. Rook, five. Queen, nine.
So be careful! Never give away your big queen just to catch a little pawn.
Points can help you see who is ahead. Pretend you played white, and you caught these two black pieces. A rook and a pawn.
The rook is five.
And one more for the pawn makes six. Six points!
Quiz time! You caught the black queen. Your friend caught a knight and a pawn. Who has more points? Have a think.

quiz.why: Counting points: a queen (9) against a knight and a pawn (3 + 1).

beats.say: You do! The queen is nine points. The knight and the pawn are three and one, which is only four.
One more. Here is one rook, or a knight with two pawns. Which pile has more points?

quiz.why: Counting points: a rook (5) against a knight and two pawns (3 + 1 + 1).

beats.say: Trick question! They have the same. The rook is five. The knight is three, plus two pawns, makes five too. More pieces does not always mean more points!
Great job! Now you know the points. Pawn one, knight three, bishop three, rook five, queen nine. Next time, we will see if we remember the main rules. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Playtime
teaches: The pawn moves straight forward, captures diagonally, and never goes backward; on its first move it may take a giant step of two squares.
The pawn has two special moves: promotion and en passant.
The knight moves in an L shape and jumps over pieces; it is the only piece that jumps in a normal move. It is worth three points.
The bishop slides diagonally as far as it likes, stays on one colour all game, and is worth three points.
The rook slides in straight lines and is worth five points.
The queen moves straight like a rook and diagonally like a bishop, but not like a knight; she is worth nine points.
The king moves one square in any direction (castling is his one two-step move); he has no points but is the most important piece.
Term: check — the king is attacked; it must be fixed right away.
There are three ways out of check: move the king, block, or capture the attacker.
Term: checkmate — the king is in check and none of the three ways out works; the game is over.
Term: castling — the king takes two steps toward a rook, and the rook hops over to stand beside him; this rook hop is the one exception to 'only the knight jumps'.
You may castle only if the king and that rook have not moved and the squares between are empty; not out of check, and not through or into danger.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Are you ready to play a real game of chess? First, let's make sure we remember the main rules. Ready? Here we go!
Here is the whole chess army, all lined up and ready. Let's visit each piece, one by one.
The pawn steps straight forward, and catches on the slant. It never goes backward. On its very first move, it may take a giant step of two squares.
It knows two magic tricks. Promotion, and en passant. And it is worth one point.
The knight hops in the shape of a letter L. No other piece moves like that.
And the knight has a special trick. It hops over anything in its way. Watch!
Hop! Over the wall. The knight is worth three points.
The bishop slides on the slants, as far as it likes.
It stays on squares of one colour for the whole game. The bishop is worth three points, just like the knight.
The rook slides in straight lines. Up and down, and side to side.
The rook is worth five points.
The queen can go straight like a rook, and on the slants like a bishop. Every direction! Only the knight's L hop is not hers.
She is the strongest piece of all, and she is worth nine points.
The king can go any way he likes, but only one small step at a time. There is one special move where he takes two steps. We will see it soon!
He has no points, because he is never taken off the board. But he is the most important piece of all. Always keep your king safe!
When a king is attacked, that is called check. Here, the black rook is attacking the white king. White must fix it right away.
There are three ways to get out of check. Let's see them all.
One. The king can step out of the way, to a safe square.
Two. Another piece can step in the way, like a wall.
Hop! The knight blocks the rook.
Three. Somebody can catch the piece that is attacking.
Gotcha! The bishop catches the rook. The king is safe again.
But what if the king is attacked, and none of those three ways work? Watch the black rook.
Check! The king cannot step away, nobody can block, and nobody can catch the rook. That is checkmate, and the game is over.
One more special move helps keep the king safe. It is called castling.
The king takes two steps toward the rook. That is his special two-step move! Then the rook hops over him to stand beside him.
The rook hops over the king only when castling. That is the one exception. In every other move, only the knight can do that. Now the king is snug behind his pawns.
You may only castle if the king and that rook have not moved yet, and every square between them is empty. You cannot castle to escape check, and the king may not walk through danger or into danger.
Quiz time! Which of these pieces is worth five points? Pause the video and point to it.

quiz.why: Naming the piece worth five points (the rook).

beats.say: The rook! The rook is worth five points. Well done!
One more. In a normal move, which of these pieces can jump right over other pieces?

quiz.why: Naming the rule that only the knight jumps in a normal move.

beats.say: The knight! In a normal move, only the knight jumps. When castling, the rook hops over the king, and that is the one exception.
Great job! You remember the main rules. Before we play, there is one more thing to learn. How to be a good chess player at the table. See you next time!

lessons.title: Chess Etiquette
teaches: Term: etiquette — good manners at the chess table.
Shake hands and say good luck before the game.
Chess is a quiet game: no shouting, silly noises, or talking to distract the other player.
Term: touch move — if you touch one of your pieces on purpose, you must move it, if it has a move.
Think first, touch second.
If you touch one of the other player's pieces on purpose and can capture it, you must capture it.
To straighten a piece without having to move it, say I adjust on your turn before touching it.
After the game, shake hands and say well done, even if you lost.
If you win, do not show off or tease; say thank you for the game.
When you finish, put all the pieces back on their starting squares.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will not learn a new move. We will learn how to be a kind and polite chess player.
Being polite at the chess table has a special name. It is called etiquette. Etiquette means good manners.
Rule number one. Before the game starts, shake hands with the other player, and say good luck. That shows you are a good sport.
Rule number two. Chess is a quiet game. Sit nicely and think. No shouting, no silly noises, and no talking to put your friend off.
Rule number three is a big one. It is called touch move. If you touch one of your pieces on purpose, you must move that piece, if it has a move.
So you touched the knight on purpose? Then the knight must move. Hop!
That is why you think first, and touch second. Keep your hands still until you have decided.
There is a rule for the other player's pieces too. If you touch one of their pieces on purpose, and you are able to catch it, then you must catch it.
Here, white touched the black knight on purpose, and the bishop can catch it. So the bishop must catch it. Gotcha! And the bishop is safe there.
What if a piece is wobbly and you only want to put it straight? On your turn, say, I adjust, before you touch it. Then you do not have to move it.
Rule number four. When the game ends, shake hands again and say, well done. Do this even if you lost. That is very grown up!
And if you win, do not show off or tease. Just smile, and say thank you for the game.
Rule number five. When you have finished, put all the pieces back where they start. Then you know nothing is lost, and the board is ready for next time.
Let's look at the back row. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. All home!
Quiz time! You touched your knight on purpose. But now you wish you had moved a pawn instead. What must you do? Have a think.

quiz.why: The touch-move rule: a piece touched on purpose must move if it can.

beats.say: You must move the knight! You touched it on purpose, and it can move, so it has to move. That is the touch move rule.
One more. You played a hard game, and you lost. What do you do now?

quiz.why: Good manners after a game: shake hands.

beats.say: You shake hands, and say well done. Good manners, win or lose!
Great job! Now you know how to be a kind chess player. And did you know? Sometimes nobody wins at all. Next time, we will find out how. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Ways to Draw
teaches: Term: draw — nobody wins and nobody loses; a tie.
Term: stalemate — the player to move cannot move at all, but the king is not attacked; it is a draw.
When you are winning, be careful not to give stalemate.
On your turn, with no legal move for any piece: if the king is attacked it is checkmate; if the king is not attacked it is stalemate, a draw.
When only the two kings are left, nobody can checkmate, so it is a draw.
A king with only one bishop or one knight can never checkmate against a king that is all alone, so that is a draw too.
You can offer a draw; if the other player says yes the game is a draw, and if no you keep playing.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Did you know that sometimes, nobody wins a chess game? Today we will find out how.
When nobody wins and nobody loses, we call it a draw. A draw is a tie. Both players are equal.
Look at this board. White has a king and a big queen. Black only has a king. White is winning, and wants to checkmate.
White moves the queen here. Now it is black's turn. Let's look at the black king.
Is the black king being attacked right now? No! He is safe, right where he is. So it is not check.
But can he move? This square, no. This square, no. This square, no. Every step would walk into danger.
And black has no other pieces to move. So black has no move at all, and the king is not attacked.
That is called stalemate. Stalemate is a draw! Nobody wins. Oh no, white was winning, and now it is only a tie.
Let's try again. This time, white is more careful.

The queen zooms all the way to the top row. Now the king is attacked, and nothing can save him. He has no safe square to step to, and black has no other piece to block the queen or catch her. That is checkmate. White wins!
So remember. It is your turn, and you have no move at all, with any piece. If your king is attacked, that is checkmate. If your king is not attacked, that is stalemate, and the game is a draw.
Here is another draw. Look. Only the two kings are left on the board.
A king can never walk right next to the other king. And a king all alone can never checkmate. So nobody can win. It is a draw!
Even one bishop with the king is not enough. Here the white king is in check. But look!
He steps away to safety. One bishop or one knight is too small a helper. Together with the king, it can never checkmate a king that is all alone. So that is a draw too.
Here is another way. During a game, you can ask your friend, would you like a draw?
If your friend says yes, the game ends, and it is a draw. If your friend says no, you just keep on playing.
Quiz time! It is black's turn. Is the black king attacked? Can he move anywhere? So, is this checkmate, or stalemate? Have a think.
It is black's turn. The black king is not attacked. He cannot step to any square, and black has no other piece, so black has no move at all. That is stalemate. It is a draw!
One more. Only two kings are left. Can anybody win?

quiz.why: A rule: two kings alone can never checkmate, so it is a draw.

beats.say: No! Two kings alone can never checkmate. It is a draw.

Great job! Now you know that a game can end in a draw. Stalemate, not enough pieces left to checkmate, and both players agreeing are three of the ways. Keep practicing, and have fun playing chess. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Chess Tournaments
teaches: Term: tournament — a big chess event where lots of children play lots of games.
Shake hands and say good luck before the game.
Play quietly so that every player can think.
Touch move: if you touch one of your pieces on purpose, you must move it, if it can move. Think, touch, move.
Never sneak the other player's pieces off the board; that is cheating.
Term: chess clock — a clock that counts how much thinking time each player uses, with one button for each player; after your move, press your button with the hand that moved the piece.
If something feels wrong or you are unsure of a rule, put your hand up for a grown-up helper.
When you win, say checkmate calmly and kindly; no cheering or showing off.
At the end, shake hands, win or lose, and say well done or thank you for the game.
Losing is okay; every game you lose teaches you something.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will learn about a chess tournament. That is a big chess party, where lots of children play lots of games. It is okay to feel a bit nervous. Just have fun!
Before the game starts, you shake hands with the other player, and say good luck. Being kind is part of chess.
During the game, everybody plays quietly, so that all the players can think. No chatting, and no silly faces or noises to bother the other player!
Here is a very important rule. It is called touch move. If you touch one of your pieces on purpose, you must move that piece, if it can move.
So choose your move first. Then touch the piece, and move it. Think, touch, move!
And look at this black knight. Nobody caught it, so it stays right where it is. We never sneak the other player's pieces off the board. That is cheating, and chess players never cheat.

Often there is a chess clock. It counts how much thinking time each player uses. It has one button for each player. After your move, press your button with the same hand that moved the piece. Then take your hand away.
If something feels wrong, or you are not sure about a rule, put your hand up. A grown-up helper will come and help you.
Now, look at this game. White can win right now! Can you see the move?
The rook zooms to the top. The black king is attacked, and nothing can save him. His own pawns block his way, and no black piece can block the rook or catch it. Checkmate!
When you win, you can say checkmate in a calm, kind voice. No cheering, and no showing off.
Quiz time! You picked up this knight on purpose. But oh no, now you wish you had moved the pawn! What must you do? Have a think.

quiz.why: The touch-move rule: a piece touched on purpose must move if it can.

beats.say: You must move the knight, because you touched it on purpose, and it can move. Touch move! That is why we think first, and touch second.
At the end of the game, you shake hands again, win or lose. Then say something kind, like well done, or thank you for the game.
Losing can feel sad, and that is okay. Every game you lose teaches you something new, and that makes you a stronger player.
Great job! Now you know how to be a super tournament player. Shake hands, play quietly, think before you touch, and be kind when you win or lose. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Chess Language
teaches: Every square on the board has its own name, like an address.
Term: file — a line of squares going up and down, named by a letter a to h (e.g. the e file).
Term: rank — a row of squares going across, numbered 1 to 8 (e.g. the fourth rank).
A square's name is where its file and rank meet: letter first, then number (e.g. e4).
Each piece has a one-letter name: K king, Q queen, R rook, B bishop, N knight.
The knight is N because K is already the king.
A pawn has no letter; a pawn move is said as just the square it goes to (e.g. e4).
A piece move is said as the piece letter, then the square (e.g. Nf3).
In chess books, ! marks a really good move.
In chess books, ? marks a mistake.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Did you know that chess has its own secret language? Today we will learn to speak it.
Every square on the chess board has its very own name. Just like your house has an address, so the postman can find it.

beats.big: a b c d e f g h
beats.say: Look along the bottom of the board. Each line going up has its own letter. This first line is a. Then come b, c, d, e, f, g, h.
This line going up and down is called the e file. Every square on it starts with the letter e.
Now look up the side of the board. Each row going across has its own number. This bottom row is 1. Then come 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
This row going across is called the fourth rank. Every square on it ends with the number 4.
Where the e file and the fourth rank meet, there is one special square. Its name is e4. Letter first, then number.
Let's find this knight. Go along the bottom to its letter. That is d. Now go up to its number. That is 5. The knight is on d5!
And this rook? Letter b, number 3. The rook is on b3.
Quiz time! What is the name of the square where this black queen is standing? Letter first, then number.

quiz.why: Naming a square: g6.

beats.say: It is g6! The letter g, and the number 6. Well done!
Chess players also give each piece a short name, just one letter. The king is K.
