The queen is Q.
The rook is R.
The bishop is B.
And the knight is N. Why not K? Because K is already the king! We don't want to mix them up.
And the pawn? The pawn has no letter at all. We just say the name of the square it goes to.
The pawn walks to e4. So in chess language, we just say, e4.
Now the knight jumps to f3. We say N for knight, then the square. N, f3.
One more! What letter does a bishop get, and what square is it on? Have a think.

quiz.why: Naming the bishop's letter (B) and its square (c4).

beats.say: B for bishop, on the square c4. B, c4. You are speaking chess!
Here is a fun bit. In chess books, a really good move gets a mark that looks like this. It means, wow, great move!
And a move that is a mistake gets a question mark. It means, oops, that was not a good idea.
Great job! Now you know that every square has a name, letter first and then number. And you know a letter for each piece, except the pawn, who needs no letter at all. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Getting Off to a Good Start
teaches: Term: opening — the start of the game, when you get your army ready.
Term: centre — the four squares in the very middle of the board; the most important place on the board.
Pieces in the centre can go everywhere quickly, so step one is to grab the centre.
Move the pawns in front of the king and queen two squares into the centre.
Step two: bring out the knights and bishops before the rooks and queen.
Bring knights out toward the middle, not the edge; a knight on the edge reaches only a few squares.
Step three: keep your king safe by castling.
Step four: when nothing stands between the two rooks they can help each other; move them toward the middle.
The opening is a race: get your pieces out quickly and take the best squares first.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will learn how to start a chess game really well. A good start helps you all the way through the game.
The start of a chess game has a special name. It is called the opening. In the opening, we get our army ready.
Look at these four squares in the very middle of the board. They are called the centre. The centre is the most important place on the board.
Pieces in the centre can go everywhere quickly. So step one is to grab the centre!
First, the pawn in front of the king takes a giant step of two.
And if nobody stops us, the pawn in front of the queen takes a giant step too. Two strong pawns in the middle!
Step two. Bring out your knights and bishops. They are smaller pieces, so we send them out first, before the big rooks and queen.
The knights hop out, and look toward the middle. Hop. Hop!
Then the bishops slide out too. Swoosh. Swoosh! Now our knights and bishops are all looking at the centre.
Quiz time! This knight wants to come out. Should it hop toward the middle, or to the edge of the board? Have a think.

quiz.why: The choice offered is f3 (toward the middle) or h3 (the edge); toward the middle reaches more squares.

beats.say: Toward the middle! A knight on the edge can only reach a few squares. A knight near the middle can reach lots of squares.
Hop! Good choice.
Step three. Keep your king safe! The king in the middle can get into trouble.
So the king castles. He takes two steps to the side, and the rook hops over the king to stand next to him. The king is tucked away safely near the corner.
Step four. Look at the two rooks. They want to help each other, but the queen is standing between them.
So the queen takes one little step forward, out of the way. Now nothing stands between the rooks. They can see each other and help each other.
Then the rooks move toward the middle too, behind the pawns. Now the whole army is ready!
Look at that. Pawns in the middle, knights and bishops out, king safe near the corner, and rooks ready. What a strong army!
But remember, the other player wants to do this too! So the opening is like a race. Get your pieces out quickly, and get the best squares first.
One more quiz. It is the very start of the game. Which pawn could you move first, to grab the centre? Point to it.

quiz.why: Grabbing the centre with the first move: only the king's and queen's pawns can step onto a centre square.

beats.say: The pawn in front of the king, or the pawn in front of the queen. They both step into the centre.
Giant step! Great start.
Great job! Now you know how to start a game. Grab the centre, bring out your knights and bishops, castle your king, and get your rooks ready. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Chess Maths
teaches: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9; the king is not counted.
Term: free piece — an unguarded piece you can catch without losing anything back.
Look out for lonely, unguarded pieces: they are free points.
Term: guarded — a piece is guarded when a friend can catch back if it is caught.
Keep your own pieces guarded.
Term: fair trade — both sides catch pieces worth the same points.
A trade where you win more points than you lose is good for you.
Never give away your queen just to catch a pawn; one point for nine is a very bad trade.
Add up each side's points to see who has more.
Usually only trade when you get the same or more points.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we are going to do some chess maths. Don't worry, it is fun counting!
Most pieces are worth some points. Do you remember? The little pawn is worth one point.
The knight is worth three points. The bishop is worth three points too.
The rook is worth five points.
And the mighty queen is worth nine points! She is the strongest of all.
What about the king? The king can never be caught, so we do not count him. Without the king, there is no game!
Now look. The white rook can catch the black knight. Is anybody guarding that knight?
No! The knight is all alone. Nobody can catch the rook back. That means the knight is free.
Gotcha! White wins three points, and black gets nothing. Always look out for lonely pieces. They are free points!
And that is why we keep our own pieces guarded. A guarded piece has a friend who can catch back.
Here, the white bishop can catch the black knight. But look, a black pawn is guarding the knight.
The bishop catches the knight. White wins three points.
Then the pawn catches the bishop back. Black wins three points.
Three points for white, and three points for black. That is the same! When both sides catch pieces worth the same, we call it a fair trade.
Now look at this. The white pawn can catch a black bishop. A black pawn is guarding it.
The pawn catches the bishop. White wins three points.
The black pawn catches back. But it only gets a little pawn. Black wins one point.
White won three points, and black won only one. Three is more than one, so this trade was great for white!
Quiz time! The white queen can catch this black pawn. But a black pawn is guarding it. Should the queen catch it? Have a think.

quiz.why: A yes/no trade question: catching a guarded pawn with the queen loses nine points for one, so no.

beats.say: Let's see. The queen catches the pawn. White wins one point.
Oh no! The black pawn catches the queen. Black wins nine points!
One point for white, nine points for black. That was a very bad trade. So, no! Never give away your queen just to catch a pawn.
One more quiz! Who has more points here, white or black? Pause the video, and count.

quiz.why: Counting points: white 9 + 1 = 10 against black 5 + 3 = 8.

beats.say: White has a queen, that is nine, and a pawn, that is one more. Ten points!
Black has a rook, that is five, and a bishop, that is three more. Eight points!
Ten is more than eight. White has more points. Brilliant counting!
Great job! Now you know chess maths. Catch lonely pieces for free, keep your own pieces guarded, and usually only trade when you get the same or more. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Classic Trick
teaches: Term: Scholar's Mate — a trick that can checkmate in four moves; lots of new players fall for it.
At the start, the pawn next to the king (f7 for black, f2 for white) is a weak spot, guarded only by the king.
In Scholar's Mate, the queen and a bishop gang up on the weak spot, and the queen captures there for checkmate.
A piece guarded by a friend cannot be captured by the king.
To stop the trick, block the queen's path to the weak spot or guard it.
Castle your king to safety soon.
Chasing an early queen with a pawn can be a mistake if it leaves another piece unguarded.
When one piece attacks the king and another piece at once, the check must be fixed first, so the other piece is often lost.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today you will learn a famous chess trick. It can win a game in just four moves! And then you will learn how to stop it.
This trick is called Scholar's Mate. A scholar is someone who is learning. Lots of new players fall for it, so let's make sure you don't!
Look at this black pawn, next to the king. At the start of the game, it is a weak spot.
Why? Because only the king is guarding it. Nobody else is helping. White has the very same weak spot, next to the white king.
So in this trick, white sends two pieces to gang up on that weak little pawn.
The game starts. White moves a middle pawn two steps. Black does the same.
Now the white bishop slides out. Look where it is pointing. Right at the weak spot!
Black brings out a knight. A good move.
And here comes the white queen! Now the queen and the bishop are both aiming at the weak spot.
The queen wants to catch that pawn. If she lands there, the bishop guards her, so the king cannot catch her back. Danger!
Black brings out the other knight and attacks the queen. That looks clever. But oh no, it does not protect the weak spot!
The queen catches the pawn. The king is in check. The bishop guards the queen, and the king has nowhere to run. Checkmate, in four moves!
That was quick! Now, here is the good news. You can stop this trick, if you know it is coming.
Let's go back, and play the same moves again.
Here is the danger again. The queen and the bishop are aiming at the weak spot.
Quiz time! One way to stop the trick is to block the queen's path to the weak spot. Which pawn could step forward to get in her way? Have a think.

quiz.why: The only pawn step that blocks the queen's line from h5 to f7 is g7-g6.

beats.say: This pawn! It steps forward and blocks the queen. And look, now it is attacking the queen too!
The queen runs away. But sneaky queen! She is still aiming at the weak spot. Danger again!
So black brings out the knight, right in the queen's path. Now the queen cannot reach the weak spot. Black is safe!
Remember. When the queen and bishop gang up on your weak spot, block them or guard it. And castle your king to safety soon.
One more thing to watch out for. Sometimes the queen comes out first, before the bishop.
Look at the black pawn in the middle. No black knight is guarding it yet. Now, should black push this other pawn, to chase the queen away? Have a think.

quiz.why: A yes/no question: pushing g7-g6 is a mistake because Qxe5+ then forks the king and the h8 rook.

beats.say: Let's see what happens if black does.
Oh no! The queen catches the lonely pawn. Now she attacks the king, and the rook in the corner, both at once!
One queen, attacking two things at the same time! Black must fix the check first. Then the queen catches the rook. So no, that pawn push was a mistake here.
Great job! Now you know the classic trick. Watch the weak spot next to your king, and block or guard it when the queen and bishop come. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Fork
teaches: Term: fork — one piece attacks two things at the same time.
A knight can fork the king and the queen.
When a fork gives check, the king must be saved first, so the other attacked piece is usually lost.
Forks happen in real games, even at the start; the queen can fork too.
A fork can attack three pieces at once.
Every piece can make a fork, even a pawn.
A pawn forks by attacking two pieces diagonally forward at once; the other side can usually save only one.
Look for forks in every game.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will learn a clever chess trick. It is called... the fork!
Think about the fork you eat your dinner with. It has pointy prongs. With one poke, it can grab two peas at once!
In chess, a fork is when one piece attacks two things at the same time. That is the trick!
Look at this white knight. Black has a king and a queen. Watch the knight jump!
Boing! Now the knight attacks the king, and it attacks the queen too. Two at once. That is a fork!
The king is in check, so black must save the king first. The queen has to wait.
The king runs away. But now, the queen is all alone.
Gotcha! The knight catches the queen.
Forks happen in real games, even right at the start. Do you remember this from the classic trick? Look at the white queen.
The queen catches a pawn. Now she attacks the king, and the rook in the corner, at the same time. You saw this before, and now you know its name. A queen fork!
Black must stop the check. Then the rook is still in trouble.
Gotcha! The queen grabs the rook.
Now look. Black has a king, a queen, and a rook. Can one little knight attack all three?
Yes, it can! The knight jumps here.
Let's count what it attacks. One. Two. Three! A fork with three prongs!
The king runs away, and the knight catches the queen.
Here is a surprise. Every piece can make a fork. Even the little pawn! Watch.
Step! The pawn steps forward. From here it can catch on the slant, so now it attacks the rook and the knight. A pawn fork!
Black can only save one of them. The pawn will catch the other one.
Quiz time! Where can the white knight jump to make a fork? The knight wants to poke the king and the rook together, with one hop.
Jump here! Now the knight attacks the king and the rook. Two at once!
The king runs away, and gotcha, the knight takes the rook. Well done!
One more! Can the white pawn make a fork? Have a think.
Yes! One step forward, and the pawn attacks the knight and the rook on the slant. A pawn fork!
Great job! A fork is one piece attacking two things at once, just like the prongs of a fork. Look for forks in every game. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Pin
teaches: Term: pin — an enemy piece looks at a piece along a line, and something more important stands behind it; if the pinned piece moves off the line, the piece behind gets attacked.
A piece pinned to its own king must not leave the line, because that would put the king in check.
A knight pinned to its king cannot move at all, because a knight always leaves its line.
If the piece behind is not the king, the pinned piece may move, but moving loses the piece behind; it is still called pinned.
Only the pieces that slide along long lines can pin: the queen, the rook and the bishop.
A knight pinned to its king cannot move at all, so it cannot run away from a new attack: attack it again, and you can win it even when it has a guard.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will learn another chess trick. It is called... the pin!
Have you ever put a picture on the wall with a pin? The picture stays up on the wall. But if you pull the pin out, the picture falls down!
In chess, a piece is pinned when an enemy piece looks at it along a line, and something more important hides behind it. If the pinned piece moves away, the piece behind gets attacked.
Look. Here is a black knight, and behind it, the black king. Watch the white rook.
The rook slides over. Now it looks straight up the line, at the knight, and at the king hiding behind it.
If the knight jumps away, the rook would attack the king. That is against the rules! So the knight is stuck. It is pinned.
When the king is behind, the pinned piece must not leave the line. A knight can never stay on a line, so this knight cannot move at all.
Now look at this one. A white bishop, a black knight, and behind it, the black queen.
The bishop looks along its slanty line, through the knight, all the way to the queen.
This time the knight is allowed to move. But should it? Let's see what happens.
The knight jumps away. Uh oh! Now nothing is in front of the queen.
Gotcha! The bishop catches the queen. So the knight should have stayed put. When moving is a big mistake, we still call the piece pinned.
Which pieces can pin? Only the ones that slide along long lines. The queen, the rook, and the bishop.
Let's count them. Queen. Bishop. Rook. Three pinners!
Here is a great idea. This knight is pinned to its king, so it cannot move at all. But a black pawn guards it. If the rook catches the knight, the pawn catches the rook. So attack the knight again!
The pawn steps up. Now the pawn attacks the knight too. The knight cannot move, so it cannot run away.
Black moves the king. Then gotcha! The pawn catches the knight.
The black pawn catches back. And the rook catches that pawn. White lost one little pawn, but won a knight and a pawn!
Quiz time! One black piece is pinned. Can you find it? Pause the video, and point to it.

quiz.why: Spotting which piece is pinned is not a move or square set; the answer is the knight on c6, pinned to the king by the bishop.

beats.say: It is the knight! The bishop looks through the knight to the king. So the knight is stuck. Well done!
One more! Here the black bishop has the queen behind it. Is the bishop allowed to move? Have a think.

quiz.why: Yes/no rule question: a piece pinned to something other than the king may move (answer: yes, but the queen behind it is lost).

beats.say: Yes, it is allowed, because the king is not behind it. But if it moves, the rook catches the queen. So it had better stay!
Great job! A pinned piece has something more important hiding behind it. If it moves away, that piece gets attacked. And a piece pinned to its king must not leave the line. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Skewer
teaches: Term: skewer — an attack on a big piece in front; it runs away, and the piece behind it gets caught.
A king in check must get out of the line when nothing can block or catch the attacker, leaving the piece behind him to be caught.
In a pin the smaller piece is in front; in a skewer the bigger piece is in front.
A skewer also works on two pieces worth the same: whichever one runs away, the other is caught.
Only the queen, the rook and the bishop can skewer, because they slide along long lines.
Look for enemy pieces standing on the same line.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today's chess trick is called... the skewer!
A skewer is a long stick. You can push it through a piece of fruit, and then through another piece of fruit behind it.
In chess, a skewer attacks a big piece in the front. The big piece runs away, and then we catch the piece behind it!
Look. The black king is in front, and a black knight is behind it. Watch the white rook.
The rook slides over and says check! It looks straight up the line, through the king, to the knight.
The king is in check. Nothing can get in the way of the rook, and nothing can catch it. So the king has to step out of the line.
Off it goes. But now, the knight behind is all alone.
Gotcha! The rook slides all the way up and catches the knight.
Do you remember the pin? In a pin, the small piece is in front, and the big piece hides behind.

A skewer is the other way around. The big piece is in front. It usually runs away to stay safe, and then the piece behind gets caught. If the big piece is the king, he must get out of check. When nothing can block or catch the attacker, he has to step away!
Black can make skewers too. This black bishop looks down its slanty line at two white knights.
Both knights are worth the same. So whichever knight runs away, the other one gets caught.
The front knight jumps away.
And gotcha! The bishop catches the knight behind.
Which pieces can skewer? The same three that can pin. The queen, the rook, and the bishop. They all slide along long lines.
Quiz time! The black king is in front of the black queen. Where can the white rook go to make a skewer?

quiz.why: Only Rb1 checks the king with the queen behind him on the same line; Rh5 also checks but nothing stands behind the king on that row.

beats.say: Slide over to here! Check! The rook looks through the king, at the queen.
The king runs away, and gotcha! The rook catches the queen. Well done!
One more! The white bishop, with a pawn guarding it, is looking up its slanty line. Is this a pin, or a skewer? Have a think.

quiz.why: Naming the tactic: the more valuable queen is in front of the rook, so it is a skewer.

beats.say: A skewer! The big queen is in front, and the rook is behind. If the queen runs away, the bishop catches the rook. And if she stays on the slant to guard the rook, the bishop catches her instead. If she catches the bishop, the pawn catches her. Wherever she goes, white still wins something!
Great job! A skewer attacks a big piece in front. It runs away, and we catch the piece behind. Always look for pieces standing on the same line. Bye bye!

lessons.title: The Discovered Attack or Check
teaches: Term: discovered attack — a front piece moves out of the way, and the piece behind it attacks.
Move the front piece to a square where it attacks something too, so there are two attacks at once.
Term: discovered check — a discovered attack that gives check.
After a discovered check, the opponent must save the king and has no time to save the other attacked piece.
A discovered attack does not have to be a check.
The front piece may capture a piece as it moves out of the way.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today's chess trick is a big surprise. It is called... the discovered attack!
Have you ever played peekaboo? You hide behind your hands. Then you move your hands away, and surprise! There you are!
A discovered attack is like that. One piece is hiding another piece. When the front piece moves away, surprise! The piece behind can attack.
Look at the white rook. It wants to look up the line at the black king. But its own knight is standing in the way.
So the knight should move. But where to? Let's look for the very best hop.
Jump! Peekaboo! Now the rook says check to the king. And look, the knight is attacking the queen!
When the surprise attack is a check, we call it a discovered check.
Black must save the king. There is no time to save the queen.
The king runs away, and gotcha! The knight catches the queen.
The surprise does not have to be a check. Look. The white rook would love to attack the black queen. But the knight is in the way again.
Where should the knight go? Let's find a square where it attacks something too.
Jump! Peekaboo! The rook attacks the queen, and the knight attacks the rook. Two attacks at once!
Black saves the queen. But the rook is still in trouble, and the queen cannot guard it from there.
Gotcha! The knight catches the rook.
Sneaky, right? Lots of players do not even notice the piece hiding at the back.
Quiz time! The white bishop wants to look at the black king, but the knight is in the way. Wherever the knight goes, the king will be in check. So where should the knight go to win the biggest prize?

quiz.why: Every knight move uncovers check from the bishop; only Nxc6 also wins something, the queen.

beats.say: The knight jumps onto the queen and catches her! Peekaboo, and the bishop says check. What a surprise!
One more! Which white piece is hiding the rook from the black king? Have a think.

quiz.why: Naming the blocking piece: the bishop on c8 stands between the rook and the king.

beats.say: The bishop! When the bishop moves away, peekaboo, the rook will say check.
Like this! Check!
Great job! In a discovered attack, the front piece moves away and the piece behind attacks. Move the front piece to a square where it attacks too. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Removing the Defender
teaches: Term: defender — a guard that looks after a friend; if you take the friend, the guard takes you back.
Term: removing the defender — first get rid of the guard, then catch the piece it was guarding.
Taking a guarded rook with your rook, when the guard takes back, is just a swap.
One way to get rid of a guard is to capture it.
A king can never be captured, so a guarding king must be chased away, for example with a check.
Giving up a bishop (3 points) to win a pawn and a rook (1 + 5 points) is a good trade.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today's chess trick is called... removing the defender!
A defender is a guard. It looks after a friend. If you take the friend, the guard takes you back!
So here is the trick. First, get rid of the guard. Then, the friend is all alone, and you can catch it!
Look. The white rook would love to catch the black rook.
But the black bishop is guarding it. If our rook takes, the bishop takes back. That is just a swap.
So, first, let's get rid of the guard. Our knight can catch the bishop!
Gotcha! And look, the knight also says check to the king.
The king steps away. Now the black rook has no guard!
Gotcha! The rook catches the rook, and nobody can take back. And look along the top row. Our rook says check to the king, too!
Here is another one. The white rook would love to catch the black rook.
But this time the guard is the black king. We can never take a king! So we must chase it away.
Our bishop zooms in, catches a pawn, and says check!
The king takes our bishop. But look! The king walked away from its rook.
Gotcha! Our rook catches the rook.
We gave away a bishop. That is worth three points. But we won a pawn and a rook. A rook alone is worth five points. Good trade!
Quiz time! The white rook wants to catch the black knight. Which black piece is guarding the knight?

quiz.why: Naming the defender: the bishop on c8 guards the knight on a6.

beats.say: The bishop! It guards the knight along its slanty line.
One more! Which white piece can catch the guard? Have a think.

quiz.why: Only the queen can capture the guarding bishop on c8 (with check); the rook cannot reach it.

beats.say: The queen! She zooms up and catches the bishop. Check, too!
The king steps away, and the rook catches the knight with no guard. Well done!
Great job! When a guard is in your way, catch it or chase it away. Then the friend it was guarding is all alone. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Walking the Dog
teaches: Checkmate means the king is attacked and nothing can save him, and it wins the game.
Two rooks can checkmate a lone king all by themselves.
Term: walking the dog — the two rooks take turns, step by step, pushing the lone king to the edge of the board.
Term: fence — a rook guarding a whole row, so the enemy king cannot step onto it.
While one rook is the fence, the other rook gives check on the king's row from far away, so the king cannot catch it, and the king must move away from the fence.
The rook that gave check becomes the new fence, and the rooks keep taking turns.
When the king is on the edge, a rook check along the edge row, with both rooks far from the king so he cannot catch either one, and the other rook guarding the row below, is checkmate.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will learn how two rooks can checkmate a king all by themselves. We call it... walking the dog! The rooks lead the king along, one step at a time, just like you lead a dog on a leash.
Remember, checkmate means the king is attacked, and nothing can save him. That wins the game!
Look. White has two rooks. The black king is all alone in the middle. Let's push it to the edge of the board.
One rook. Two rooks. They will take turns, like two feet walking up the stairs.
Here is a clear picture. First, one rook builds a fence.
Slide! Now the rook guards this whole row. The king cannot step onto it. That is the fence.
Now it is black's turn. The king can never come down. It can only go sideways, or up. It steps sideways.
Now the other rook steps up and says check! The king cannot stay in this row, and it cannot cross the fence. See how far away the rooks stay? Then the king can never catch them.
So the king must go up. And look, now this rook is the new fence!
Next foot! This rook steps up and says check.
Up goes the king again. Step by step, the rooks walk the king to the edge.
Step! Check!
Now the king is pushed all the way to the top row. One more check will finish the job!
Quiz time! Which rook can step up and give checkmate? Pause the video, and point to it.
This one! The rook slides to the top and says check. The other rook guards the row below. The king cannot escape. Checkmate!
One more! This rook is the fence, so it stays right where it is. Which rook should step up and give check? Have a think.

quiz.why: The fence rook on a5 must stay to keep the king off the fifth row, so only the other rook steps up: Rh6+ pushes the king up again. Ra6+ or Rd5+ give up the fence, and Rd4+ does not step up.

beats.say: The rook at the back! It slides up past the fence and says check. The king must go up again. Well done!

Great job! One rook makes a fence, the other says check, and they take turns until the king reaches the edge. Then one rook says check along the edge, and the other guards the row below. Checkmate! Keep both rooks far from the king, so he cannot catch them. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Queen and King Checkmate
teaches: Checkmate means the king is attacked and nothing can save him, and it wins the game.
A queen and king can checkmate a lone king, but the queen cannot do it by herself; her own king must help.
First put the queen close to the enemy king, but not too close: an L-shape away, like a knight's move, guarding the squares around him.
Shadow trick: every time the enemy king moves, the queen copies his move, pushing him toward the edge.
Reminder of stalemate: it is your turn, your king is not attacked, and you have no legal move at all with any piece; it is a draw.
When the enemy king is in the corner, do not take away his last square without giving check, or it is stalemate.
Keep the enemy king locked on the edge with the queen, and walk your own king up to help.
Checkmate: the queen goes right next to the enemy king, and her own king stands behind her, keeping her safe.
Another checkmate: the queen checks along the edge row while her king guards the squares in front of the enemy king.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today the queen and the king work as a team, to checkmate the other king. Let's learn a checkmate!
Remember, checkmate means the king is attacked, and nothing can save him. Checkmate wins the game!
Look. White has a queen and a king. Black only has a king. Can White win? Yes! But the queen needs a helper.
The queen cannot checkmate all by herself. Her own king must come and help her. They are a team.
First, the queen moves close to the black king, but not too close. Look, she is one L-shape away from him, just like a knight's move.
Now the black king cannot step on any of these squares. The queen is guarding them all.
Here is a fun trick. Every time the black king moves, the queen copies him, just like a shadow.
The king steps up and to the left. So the queen steps up and to the left too!
Again! The king steps. The queen copies.
The king steps sideways. The queen steps sideways. He is being pushed toward the edge of the board.
Now the black king hides in the corner. Should the queen copy him again? Be careful! Have a think.

quiz.why: Yes/no judgement: copying the king (Qc7) would be stalemate, so the answer is no.

beats.say: If the queen copies, look. The black king is not in check. But every square next to him is guarded. He cannot move at all!
Remember stalemate? It is Black's turn. The black king is not attacked, and Black has no legal move at all, with any piece. That is stalemate. It is a draw, so nobody wins!
Oh no, we wanted to win! Let's go back and try again.
This time, the queen steps here instead. Now the black king still has one square to walk to. Phew! No stalemate.
The queen keeps the black king locked on the top row. Now White's king walks up to help. Step, step.
Step, step, step. The black king can only walk back and forth, back and forth.
The black king has just one square left. Into the corner he goes.
Quiz time! It is White's turn. Can the queen give checkmate in just one move? Find a square where she says check, and nobody can save the black king.

Here! The queen moves right next to the black king. Check! Did you pick the square below him? That is checkmate too. Or did you slide her along the top row, to one of these squares? Also checkmate! Well done!
Can the black king take the queen? No! White's king is guarding her. Can he run away? No! Checkmate!
That is the big secret. The queen goes right next to the enemy king, and her own king stands behind her, keeping her safe.
Now let's look closely at the other way, along the top row. We go back to before the queen moved.
The queen slides to the top row. Check! White's king guards the squares in front. Nothing can save the black king. Checkmate again!
Great job! Remember: the queen pushes the king to the edge, watch out for stalemate, and bring your own king to help. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Box Them In
teaches: A rook and king can checkmate a lone king.
A rook moves in straight lines, so it makes a wall that the enemy king is not allowed to cross.
Term: box — the area the rook's walls keep the enemy king inside.
Rule: first try to shrink the box with the rook; if you cannot, walk your king nearer.
Only shrink the box when the rook will be safe; your king can stand next to the rook to guard it.
In the corner, shrinking the box without giving check can be stalemate: it is Black's turn, his king is not attacked, and he has no legal move at all with any piece; that is a draw, a tie.
Near the corner, move the king instead; the rook can go far away along its line and still keep the wall.
Checkmate: the rook checks along the edge row while your king guards the squares in front of the enemy king.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today a rook and a king work together. They push the other king into a smaller and smaller box, until checkmate. Let's go!
White has a rook and a king. Black only has a king. White wins by checkmating him.
A rook moves in straight lines. So a rook can make a wall. The black king is not allowed to cross it.
A little later, the board looks like this. Look at the two walls. One goes up, and one goes sideways.
The black king is inside a box! The rook's walls keep him from crossing out of it.
Here is our rule. First, try to shrink the box with the rook. No way to shrink it? Then walk your king nearer.
The black king steps here.
Now the rook slides over, and the box gets smaller! White's king stands next to the rook, keeping it safe.
Black steps up.
Can the box get smaller now? The rook could move up here. But then the black king could step over and catch it, because nobody would guard it.
So, White moves the king closer instead.
Black steps away.
Now the box can get smaller again! The rook moves up, and the white king guards it.
Smaller box, or king closer. Again and again. The box shrinks, until the black king is squeezed into a corner.
Like this! It is Black's turn, and he has only one square to go to. The corner.
Into the corner he goes. Now be careful!
What if the rook makes the box smaller, to here? The black king is not in check. He cannot catch the rook, because the white king guards it. He has no safe square at all!
Remember stalemate? It is Black's turn. The black king is not attacked, and Black has no legal move at all, with any piece. That is stalemate. It is a draw, a tie. Oh no! We wanted to win.
Let's go back. This time, White moves the king, not the rook.
The white king steps here.
The black king must step out of the corner. That is his only move.
Now the rook walks far away, down its line. Look, the black king still cannot cross this wall.
Back into the corner he goes. Again, it was his only move.
Quiz time! Can you find the checkmate? Pause the video and have a think.
Rook to the top row. Check! The black king cannot run, because the white king guards the squares in front. Checkmate!
Great job! Remember: shrink the box, or walk your king nearer. And near the corner, always check for stalemate. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Puzzle Section 1: Winning Material
teaches: In these puzzles, White moves first and can catch a black piece.
Term: winning material — catching pieces and keeping your own pieces safe.
If a piece is guarded, catch the guard first, then catch the piece it was guarding.
When the enemy queen and king stand on the same slanting line, a bishop can pin the queen to her king.
Giving a bishop to catch a queen is a great trade.
Attacking two pieces at once is a fork; the opponent can save only one of them.
A piece pinned to its king may move only along the pin line; if every square on that line still loses it, it cannot get away safely.
A knight check that also attacks the queen can win the queen.
When a piece moves out of the way, a piece behind it can attack too.
Keep looking for pieces with no guard.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today is puzzle day! In every puzzle, White moves first, and White can catch a black piece.
Catching pieces and keeping your own pieces safe is called winning material. Ready? Let's go!
Puzzle one. Our rook would love to catch this black bishop.
But look. The black knight is guarding the bishop. What should White do first? Have a think.

quiz.why: Remove the defender: Bxf6+ catches the knight that guards the bishop on d5, and the rook wins that bishop next.

beats.say: Catch the guard first! Our bishop takes the knight, and says check.
The black king takes our bishop. But now, who is guarding the black bishop? Nobody!
Gotcha! First catch the guard. Then catch the piece it was guarding.
Puzzle two. Look at the black queen and the black king. They are standing on the same slanting line. Can you trap the queen?

quiz.why: Bb2 attacks the queen and pins her to the king on g7, so she cannot escape the slanting line and is lost.

beats.say: The bishop steps here. Now it attacks the queen. Can she get away safely? No! If she leaves this slanting line, the bishop would attack her king. And every square along the line still loses her.
This is called a pin. The queen is pinned to her king, like a picture pinned to the wall.
And if the black queen catches our bishop, our queen is ready.
Snap, and snap! White gave a bishop, and caught a queen. What a great trade!
Puzzle three. Two black rooks are standing with one empty square between them. Can a little white pawn help us?

quiz.why: c4 forks the two rooks on b5 and d5; one of them is lost.

beats.say: The pawn takes a giant step of two squares! Now it attacks both rooks at the same time.
Attacking two pieces at once is called a fork. Black can only save one of them.
And this rook cannot run away at all, because our queen would then attack the black king. White will catch a rook!
Last puzzle. Look at the black queen. Nobody is guarding her. Can you find a way to catch her?

quiz.why: Both knight checks win the unguarded queen on d5: Nf6+ forks the king on h7 and the queen, and Ng5+ gives check while uncovering the white queen on f3 against d5. Black must answer the check, so the queen falls next move (Qxd5, or Nxd5 after Nf6+ if the king steps away).

beats.say: The knight jumps here, and says check! It attacks the king and the queen at the same time.
And look! The knight was standing in our queen's way. Now our queen can see the black queen too.
Black has to stop the check. The pawn catches our knight.
But then our queen catches the black queen. Gotcha!
Did you find a different jump? The knight can also hop here, and say check! And again our queen can see the black queen.
The pawn catches our knight to stop the check. But our queen catches the black queen. That way works too!
Great job, puzzle solver! You learned to catch the guard, to pin, and to fork. Keep looking for pieces with no guard. Bye bye!

lessons.title: Puzzle Section 2: Mate in One
teaches: Term: mate in one — a puzzle where you must checkmate the king in just one move.
Checkmate means the king is attacked and nothing can save him.
A checking piece right next to the enemy king must be guarded, or the king can take it.
A king's own pieces can block his escape squares.
The king cannot escape to squares on the checking piece's line.
A piece that moves out of the way can also guard the king's escape squares.
When one piece moves out of the way and a hidden piece behind it gives check, that is a discovered check.
Two pieces can give check at the same time.
With two checks at once, blocking or catching one checker cannot help, because the other check is still there; only a king move could.
To find checkmate, look for a check, then ask three questions: can the king step to a safe square, can anyone block, can anyone catch the attacker? If every answer is no, it is checkmate.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! More puzzles today. These are called mate in one. You must checkmate the black king in just one move!
Remember, checkmate means the king is attacked, and nothing can save him. White moves first in every puzzle. Ready?
Puzzle one. Can you find a checkmate? Here is a hint. Our queen wants to get right next to the black king. Where can she go, and still be safe?
Not here. The black rook would catch her.
Here! The queen says check. And our little pawn guards her, so the king cannot take her.
The king cannot step here, or here. His own pieces block the other squares. Checkmate!

Did you find a different checkmate? Our rook can zoom all the way up to the top row. Check! The king cannot step along that row. And g7 is guarded twice, by our queen and by our pawn. Nobody can block or catch the rook. Checkmate too!
Puzzle two. The black king has lots of his own pieces around him. Can our bishop checkmate him?
The bishop slides all the way here. Check!
These squares are on the bishop's line. And his own pieces fill up every other square, like a crowded room. Checkmate!
Puzzle three. Our bishop is aiming at the black king. But our own rook is standing in the way!
Where can the rook go, to make checkmate? Have a think.
The rook slides out of the way, and catches a pawn. Now the bishop says check!
And the rook guards this whole line, so the king has nowhere to run. Checkmate!
When one piece moves out of the way, and a hidden piece behind it says check, that is called a discovered check.
Last puzzle. Look at this rook of ours, far away at the bottom. It is on the same line as the black king. Can a little pawn make checkmate?
The pawn catches on the slant! Now the pawn says check, and our rook says check too. Two checks at once!

The king cannot take the pawn, because our bishop guards it. And he cannot step forward, because of our rook. Could Black block a check? That cannot help! With two checks at once, blocking one, or catching one checker, still leaves the other check. Only a king move could help, and he has none. Checkmate!

Great job, checkmate hunter! Always look for a check. Then ask three questions. Can the king step to a safe square? Can anyone block? Can anyone catch the attacker? If every answer is no, it is checkmate! Bye bye!

lessons.title: Master Game
teaches: Paul Morphy was a great chess master who lived long ago.
At the start, push a middle pawn and bring out your knights and bishops.
Pushing pawns while your pieces are still asleep at home is a mistake.
A master may give away pieces to attack the enemy king while the opponent's pieces are not ready.
Castling queenside hides the king on the side and brings the rook to the middle, ready to attack.
Giving away the queen with check can force a capture that opens the way to checkmate.
Bring out all your pieces early and make them work as a team.

beats.say: Hello, chess friends! Today we will watch a real game, played long, long ago, by a great chess master called Paul Morphy.
He played this game at the opera, while the show was going on! Two men teamed up together to play against him.
Paul Morphy has the white pieces. Let's watch!
Both sides push a middle pawn. White brings out a knight. Black guards his pawn.
White pushes a pawn to the middle. Black's bishop slides out, to bother the white knight.
Snap, snap, snap, snap! Pieces catch each other.
Look. White's queen is already out, ready to play. But Black's knights are still asleep at home.
White's bishop comes out. Black brings out a knight.
The queen moves here. Now she attacks this pawn. And this pawn, next to the black king? The bishop attacks it, and the queen stands right behind the bishop on the same slant, backing it up. A team!

Black's queen comes to guard the pawn next to his king. White calmly brings out another knight. Then Black moves a pawn out of his queen's way. Now she can see along her row, and she guards the other pawn too.
White's last bishop comes out. Now all of White's knights and bishops are out, ready to fight!
But Black pushes a pawn, instead of waking up his sleepy pieces. That is a mistake. Watch what Morphy does!
Wow! Morphy gives away his knight, just for a pawn. Why would he do that?
Because now his bishop slides in, and says check!
Black blocks the check with a knight.
Then White castles. The king takes two steps to the side, and the rook hops over the king, to the middle. Now the king is hidden, and the rook is ready to attack.
Black brings a rook over, to guard the knight.
Morphy's rook catches the black knight. But the black rook takes it back! So Morphy gives a rook for a knight.
Another white rook rushes over. Black moves his queen, hoping to swap queens.
The bishop takes the rook. Check!
The black knight takes the bishop.
Now Morphy found an amazing move. His queen goes all the way to the top row, and says check. Can you find it? Have a think.

quiz.why: Morphy's Qb8+ gives the queen away to force mate: Nxb8 Rd8#. Qxe6+ also checks but is not on the top row and leads to no mate.

beats.say: The queen zooms all the way here, and says check! She gives herself away!
The black knight has to take her. Now look, the knight has left its square.
The rook slides in, and says check! The bishop guards the rook. The king cannot escape. Checkmate!
Morphy gave away lots of pieces. But every piece he had left was out and working together. That is how a master plays!
Great job! Remember Morphy's lesson: bring out all your pieces early, and make them work as a team. Bye bye!

puzzles.context: Now, look at this game. White can win right now! Can you see the move?
puzzles.explanation: The rook zooms to the top. The black king is attacked, and nothing can save him. His own pawns block his way, and no black piece can block the rook or catch it. Checkmate!

puzzles.title: Chess Tournaments · 2

exercise.prompt: You picked up the knight on purpose. What must you do?

puzzles.context: Quiz time! You picked up this knight on purpose. But oh no, now you wish you had moved the pawn! What must you do? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: The touch-move rule: a piece touched on purpose must move if it can.

puzzles.title: Chess Language · 1

exercise.prompt: What is the queen’s square?

puzzles.context: Quiz time! What is the name of the square where this black queen is standing? Letter first, then number.
puzzles.explanation: Naming a square: g6.

puzzles.title: Chess Language · 2

exercise.prompt: How do you name this bishop and its square?

puzzles.context: One more! What letter does a bishop get, and what square is it on? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Naming the bishop's letter (B) and its square (c4).

puzzles.title: Getting Off to a Good Start · 1
puzzles.topic: Getting Off to a Good Start

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! This knight wants to come out. Should it hop toward the middle, or to the edge of the board? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: The choice offered is f3 (toward the middle) or h3 (the edge); toward the middle reaches more squares.

puzzles.title: Getting Off to a Good Start · 2
puzzles.topic: Getting Off to a Good Start

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: One more quiz. It is the very start of the game. Which pawn could you move first, to grab the centre? Point to it.
puzzles.explanation: Grabbing the centre with the first move: only the king's and queen's pawns can step onto a centre square.

puzzles.title: Chess Maths · 1

exercise.prompt: Should the queen take the pawn guarded by another pawn?

puzzles.context: Quiz time! The white queen can catch this black pawn. But a black pawn is guarding it. Should the queen catch it? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: A yes/no trade question: catching a guarded pawn with the queen loses nine points for one, so no.

puzzles.title: Chess Maths · 2

exercise.prompt: Who has more points? Do not count the kings.

puzzles.context: One more quiz! Who has more points here, white or black? Pause the video, and count.
puzzles.explanation: Counting points: white 9 + 1 = 10 against black 5 + 3 = 8.

puzzles.title: The Classic Trick · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! One way to stop the trick is to block the queen's path to the weak spot. Which pawn could step forward to get in her way? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: The only pawn step that blocks the queen's line from h5 to f7 is g7-g6.

puzzles.title: The Classic Trick · 2

exercise.prompt: Should Black push g7–g6 with the central pawn unguarded?

puzzles.context: Look at the black pawn in the middle. No black knight is guarding it yet. Now, should black push this other pawn, to chase the queen away? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: A yes/no question: pushing g7-g6 is a mistake because Qxe5+ then forks the king and the h8 rook.

puzzles.title: The Fork · 1

exercise.prompt: Make a fork. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! Where can the white knight jump to make a fork? The knight wants to poke the king and the rook together, with one hop.
puzzles.explanation: Jump here! Now the knight attacks the king and the rook. Two at once!

puzzles.title: The Fork · 2

exercise.prompt: Make a fork. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: One more! Can the white pawn make a fork? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Yes! One step forward, and the pawn attacks the knight and the rook on the slant. A pawn fork!

puzzles.title: The Pin · 1

exercise.prompt: Tap the pinned black piece.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! One black piece is pinned. Can you find it? Pause the video, and point to it.
puzzles.explanation: Spotting which piece is pinned is not a move or square set; the answer is the knight on c6, pinned to the king by the bishop.

puzzles.title: The Pin · 2

exercise.prompt: Is the bishop legally allowed to move, even if the queen is lost?

puzzles.context: One more! Here the black bishop has the queen behind it. Is the bishop allowed to move? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Yes/no rule question: a piece pinned to something other than the king may move (answer: yes, but the queen behind it is lost).

puzzles.title: The Skewer · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! The black king is in front of the black queen. Where can the white rook go to make a skewer?
puzzles.explanation: Only Rb1 checks the king with the queen behind him on the same line; Rh5 also checks but nothing stands behind the king on that row.

puzzles.title: The Skewer · 2

exercise.prompt: Is this tactic a pin or a skewer?

puzzles.context: One more! The white bishop, with a pawn guarding it, is looking up its slanty line. Is this a pin, or a skewer? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Naming the tactic: the more valuable queen is in front of the rook, so it is a skewer.

puzzles.title: The Discovered Attack or Check · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! The white bishop wants to look at the black king, but the knight is in the way. Wherever the knight goes, the king will be in check. So where should the knight go to win the biggest prize?
puzzles.explanation: Every knight move uncovers check from the bishop; only Nxc6 also wins something, the queen.

puzzles.title: The Discovered Attack or Check · 2

exercise.prompt: Tap the white piece hiding the rook’s attack.

puzzles.context: One more! Which white piece is hiding the rook from the black king? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Naming the blocking piece: the bishop on c8 stands between the rook and the king.

puzzles.title: Removing the Defender · 1

exercise.prompt: Tap the black piece guarding the knight.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! The white rook wants to catch the black knight. Which black piece is guarding the knight?
puzzles.explanation: Naming the defender: the bishop on c8 guards the knight on a6.

puzzles.title: Removing the Defender · 2

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: One more! Which white piece can catch the guard? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Only the queen can capture the guarding bishop on c8 (with check); the rook cannot reach it.

puzzles.title: Walking the Dog · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! Which rook can step up and give checkmate? Pause the video, and point to it.
puzzles.explanation: This one! The rook slides to the top and says check. The other rook guards the row below. The king cannot escape. Checkmate!

puzzles.title: Walking the Dog · 2

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: One more! This rook is the fence, so it stays right where it is. Which rook should step up and give check? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: The fence rook on a5 must stay to keep the king off the fifth row, so only the other rook steps up: Rh6+ pushes the king up again. Ra6+ or Rd5+ give up the fence, and Rd4+ does not step up.

puzzles.title: Queen and King Checkmate · 1

exercise.prompt: Should the queen copy the king again?

puzzles.context: Now the black king hides in the corner. Should the queen copy him again? Be careful! Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Yes/no judgement: copying the king (Qc7) would be stalemate, so the answer is no.

puzzles.title: Queen and King Checkmate · 2

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! It is White's turn. Can the queen give checkmate in just one move? Find a square where she says check, and nobody can save the black king.
puzzles.explanation: Here! The queen moves right next to the black king. Check! Did you pick the square below him? That is checkmate too. Or did you slide her along the top row, to one of these squares? Also checkmate! Well done!

puzzles.title: Box Them In · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Quiz time! Can you find the checkmate? Pause the video and have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Rook to the top row. Check! The black king cannot run, because the white king guards the squares in front. Checkmate!

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 1: Winning Material · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: But look. The black knight is guarding the bishop. What should White do first? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Remove the defender: Bxf6+ catches the knight that guards the bishop on d5, and the rook wins that bishop next.

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 1: Winning Material · 2

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Puzzle two. Look at the black queen and the black king. They are standing on the same slanting line. Can you trap the queen?
puzzles.explanation: Bb2 attacks the queen and pins her to the king on g7, so she cannot escape the slanting line and is lost.

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 1: Winning Material · 3

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Puzzle three. Two black rooks are standing with one empty square between them. Can a little white pawn help us?
puzzles.explanation: c4 forks the two rooks on b5 and d5; one of them is lost.

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 1: Winning Material · 4

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Last puzzle. Look at the black queen. Nobody is guarding her. Can you find a way to catch her?
puzzles.explanation: Both knight checks win the unguarded queen on d5: Nf6+ forks the king on h7 and the queen, and Ng5+ gives check while uncovering the white queen on f3 against d5. Black must answer the check, so the queen falls next move (Qxd5, or Nxd5 after Nf6+ if the king steps away).

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 2: Mate in One · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Puzzle one. Can you find a checkmate? Here is a hint. Our queen wants to get right next to the black king. Where can she go, and still be safe?
puzzles.explanation: Not here. The black rook would catch her.

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 2: Mate in One · 2

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Puzzle two. The black king has lots of his own pieces around him. Can our bishop checkmate him?
puzzles.explanation: The bishop slides all the way here. Check!

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 2: Mate in One · 3

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Where can the rook go, to make checkmate? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: The rook slides out of the way, and catches a pawn. Now the bishop says check!

puzzles.title: Puzzle Section 2: Mate in One · 4

exercise.prompt: Find a checkmate. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Last puzzle. Look at this rook of ours, far away at the bottom. It is on the same line as the black king. Can a little pawn make checkmate?
puzzles.explanation: The pawn catches on the slant! Now the pawn says check, and our rook says check too. Two checks at once!

puzzles.title: Master Game · 1

exercise.prompt: Find a strong move. Select a piece, then its destination.

puzzles.context: Now Morphy found an amazing move. His queen goes all the way to the top row, and says check. Can you find it? Have a think.
puzzles.explanation: Morphy's Qb8+ gives the queen away to force mate: Nxb8 Rd8#. Qxe6+ also checks but is not on the top row and leads to no mate.
